subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERY-PROCESSING OF FISH IN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister for International Trade. The fishing industry in British Columbia is concerned, as all Canadians should be, at the prospect of losing our right to process Canadian salmon and herring in Canada. With regard to ongoing negotiations with the United States, will the Minister assure the House that his Government will reject the so-called Murphy 2 proposal which would allow the Americans to purchase fish directly from B.C. vessels without a Canadian landing requirement?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERY-PROCESSING OF FISH IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Fisheries and I have been engaged for a number of months now in dealing with the situation cited by the Hon. Member.
A GATT panel found that the present regulations, soon to be revoked, prohibiting any export of certain kinds of salmon from British Columbia, were contrary to the GATT rules. We accepted the GATT panel report.
We have put an alternate plan before the American authorities, one which we believe to be GATT consistent, involving a landing requirement in British Columbia. That is the plan that we are going with. We do not
Oral Question Period
propose to change it. In our view, and according to the experts who advise us, it is a GATT-consistent landing requirement necessary to ensure proper management of the B.C. salmon resource. That is the plan with which we will be proceeding.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is addressed to the same Minister.
He mentioned salmon but not herring. There is some concern about herring as well. With respect to both, the previous Minister for International Trade said on March 21 in this House that salmon and herring caught off the Pacific Coast will be landed in Canada in order to ensure accurate catch reporting, inspection, grading, and quality control.
Will the Minister assure us at this time that his Government will not sell the B.C. fishing industry down the free trade deal river as it did with B.C. grape growers?
Hear, hear!

speechtext:

Last July 18 regarding the Hibernia project he said that a binding agreement, and I quote, "would be implemented as expeditiously as possible, but in any event no later than March 31, 1989. It is anticipated that it will be done much sooner than that, since most of the hurdles have been overcome".

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: HIBERNIA OIL FIELD DEVELOPMENT-DATE OF CONCLUDING BINDING AGREEMENT

Mr. Speaker, I have answered this question before. The hon. gentleman can read it in the record.
Let me give him the salient points again. He knows that there were three issues. The first was in terms of the legal requirements. The second concerns the testing of financial markets. The third concerns the best industrial benefits with the best modem technology. I think I mentioned that yesterday in the House. That has not changed 24 hours later. That is what we are working on.
When we have a binding agreement I will obviously announce it in the House. I will not give him a specific date. All the parties, namely, the Government of Newfoundland, the Government of Canada, and the sponsors of the consortium are all working toward that goal.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Energy gives us information but he fails to tell us exactly when we can expect this binding agreement. The Minister for International Trade said on July 19 that they will all be legally bound by the end of March, referring to the companies involved, and: "In the meantime, we are morally bound. We are completely bound".
If the Government is bound, surely it can tell us when the people of Newfoundland can expect a binding agreement to secure this very important project. Or is this just another assurance similar to the assurance the Minister for International Trade gave on unemployment insurance?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am certainly very pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate as our Government begins the second session of the Thirty-fourth Parliament. I would first like to take this opportunity to commend the Government of which I am extremely proud on its past performance, a performance that will be equalled if not surpassed in the next four years, and I am sure many more years to come. I compliment our Government on its achievements in initiating so many new policies encompassing such diverse areas.
When I was asked to speak on the Throne Speech, I asked myself what is a Throne Speech, and I looked up a definition. I quote from the book Government of Canada written by Dawson. The Throne Speech:
- is a statement, drafted by the Prime Minister and approved by the cabinet, which reviews concisely the state of the nation and recites in fairly general terms the program which the cabinet proposes to Parliament in the upcoming session.
As I see it, the Throne Speech outlined a course of action for the future while reflecting on the past accomplishments of this Government. As a result of the endeavours of our Government, Canada's economy grew faster last year than those of the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, France and Italy. In real terms, our economy grew by 4.3 per cent. The Canadian economy will continue to grow with increased international trade under the direction and leadership of this Government.
Since 1984, Canada's job creation record has been the best of any major OECD nation. The unemployment rate was cut from 11.2 per cent to 7.8 per cent in December, more recently to 7.6 per cent and it was just announced last Friday that it was 7.5 per cent. Under the previous Liberal Government, in 1982, this country experienced record high unemployment. That Liberal Government had allowed youth unemployment to climb to unacceptable levels, while our Government cut youth employment by one-third.
Our Government is dedicated to maintaining for the youth of this nation a prosperous labour market in which to grow and participate with a sense of accomplishment. This Government's dedication is very evident in my riding. For years, the employment situation in York- Simcoe and surrounding ridings has been excellent.
April 13, 1989

The supervisor of the Canadian Employment Centre for Students recently informed me of the tremendous employment prospects for students this summer. The original function of the centre was to find suitable jobs for students. However, and particularly this summer, its function seems to be finding enough students to fill the numerous vacancies businesses have posted at the centre. The students of York-Simcoe are extremely fortunate because not only are they being given an opportunity to earn money for university and college expenses, but they are gaining valuable work experience and getting a glimpse of the work and business world of their future.
The key words used in the Throne Speech were "building", "preparing", "protection", "caring" and "sustainable development". These words are descriptive of a Government that shows every indication of providing the next and future generations with a standard of living comparable to the one we cherish today as one of the highest in the world. However, our standard of living, the strength of the economy, the unemployment level will mean nothing to our children and grandchildren if we do not make provisions to ensure them of an environment in which life flourishes, not diminishes.
The commitment our Government made four years ago to making the environment a priority was reaffirmed in a mandate outlined in the Throne Speech. As the record shows, our Government's accomplishments in initiating environmental policies and directives have been vast. Agreements have been signed with all the provinces to cut in half acid rain causing emissions from factories by 1994. Actions were taken to have leaded gasoline emissions cut out completely by 1994. Bill C-30 was passed to improve the National Parks Act. Bill C-74 was passed to provide stricter controls on handling toxic wastes from their production to their disposal. In 1987, Canada hosted an international conference on the ozone layer in Montreal. That historic agreement, signed by more than 40 countries, is designed to reduce emissions, which destroy the ozone layer, by 50 per cent by 1999. As well, we hosted an international conference on the chemical contamination of the atmosphere which was held in Toronto in June of 1988.
As the Throne Speech outlined, our Government is going to continually develop policies that reflect the concept of sustainable development where our economic policies are not divorced from their environmental
The Address-Mr. Cole
impact. In Winnipeg, there is the creation of a centre for the international promotion of sustainable development. More information and direction will come from the round table on the environment and the economy, which is being chaired by the President of McGill University.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) has been giving me responsibilities to ensure that environmental issues are fully considered in the course of Government decision-making. There will be new regulations to limit the impact of toxic chemicals; actions to protect the arctic environment; new legislation to ensure an appropriate environmental assessment review process; negotiations, both with the United States and globally, to improve the quality of the atmosphere; and initiatives to clean up the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River.
As I stand here reflecting on and listing the many accomplishments and future directives of our Government, words to a song keep running through my mind: "Every generation blames the one before it". Under the leadership of this Government, those words will not be echoed in the minds of our children. If I may plagiarize the words of my wise colleague, the Hon. Don Mazan-kowski, "today's farmlands", today's environment, "are our children's heritage and we owe it to future generations to be wise stewards of this renewable resource"; of these precious lakes and forests; of this land.
I would like to speak a bit on the topic of a Human Resource Development Strategy and the pending necessity for the training and retraining of Canada's workforce, especially our youth.
Prior to 1986 and in the early part of 1984, businesses were able to select the best qualified, sometimes over qualified candidates, totally ignoring the less advantaged or less equipped candidate, such as high school dropouts. Fortunately, because of the leadership shown by this Government, we are experiencing record low unemployment. University, college and high school graduates are now able to find jobs better matched to their aspirations. They no longer have to settle for positions that are grossly below their academic credentials and career potentials. In many instances, graduates are able to choose the company they want to work for rather than have the company choose them. The situation has not improved that much for high school drop-outs, but we are making good strides in helping this forgotten group face and conquer the labour market.

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Cole
The contribution of our Government in helping dropouts and potential drop-outs is evident in the region of York, which is a major portion of my riding of York- Simcoe. Last August, my colleague, the Hon. Barbara McDougall, in her capacity as Minister of Employment, approved the federal Government funding of a program designed to help potential high school drop-outs in Ontario's York region.
The funding, which came from the innovative program of Canadian Jobs Strategy, has helped to fund a three-year project that established a career centre to assess and give career counselling to potential high school dropouts. The drop-out rate in the region of York is about 33 per cent. I was astonished when I heard that figure. This program is designed to give students a glimpse of what the future would be like if they dropped out of school and to provide them with an incentive to stay in school. The intent of the program is not to make students feel that university or college, in the traditional sense, is the be all and end all for everyone. The centre does, however, promote the merits of finishing high school.
The funding also helped establish the York Region Education-Industrial Foundation which identifies sectors where worker shortages exist. Employers in York region have identified skilled labour shortages as the most critical problem facing them today.
The career centre, working in co-operation with the education-industrial foundation, helps steer potential drop-outs into trades in which the foundation has identified a need for workers. The centre is also assisting graduates, disabled and minority groups find employment.
This program is just one small example of how employment and immigration, through Canada's Jobs Strategy Innovations Program, encourages the development of new ways to ensure that Canadians have meaningful employment. Its funding of innovative projects designed to keep the Canadian labour market growing demonstrates our Government's commitment to meeting the ever-changing labour needs of Canadian businesses and their potential employees.
I would like to quote the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall).
The Government knows that Canadians want to work. We will therefore use unemployment insurance funds to actively help the unemployed find jobs. There will be faster, easier access to counselling, training and re-employment programs. The unemployment insurance program will continue to be an integral part of Canada's social system.
Our goal is to improve the UI system and current labour market
programs. These improvements redirect funds to new, more effective
ways to help unemployed Canadians.
"Innovative" is a word representative of this Government, and innovation will be needed in designing future programs to meet labour market changes, especially in a time of necessary fiscal restraint. New technology is being introduced in this country at an accelerating rate. New technologies will require more sophisticated skills.
Technology coupled with the aspirations of Canada's youth to surpass the educational achievements of their parents put a tremendous onus on this Government. We are faced with a wide discrepancy between the educational aspirations of young people and the present capacity and diversity of the education system to meet these expectations. More so now than ever, the job market calls for a higher level of skill than was required for earlier generations.
My riding, York Simcoe, which is part of the fastest growing region in Canada, is already faced with an employment crisis. Developers have been "building" and "expanding" in the last few years. Towns such as Newmarket, which had a population growth of 17 per cent from 1981 to 1986, East Gwillimbury, Georgina, and other towns in this area have had major growth spurts. Eighty per cent of the increase in this region is attributed to the migration of young families within the age group of 25 to 44. My riding has a shortage of skilled workers. The 15 per cent increase between 1985 and 1986 in business establishments creates a demand for trained employees that we are still trying to meet.
The migration to my area is due in part to the expansion of the 404 which now ends in Newmarket and to the York-Durham sewage system. The increase is also due in part to the exceedingly high house prices in Toronto. The price of housing in my area is not low.
Another major reason for our continual growth is attributable to the sense of community my riding has maintained despite its rapid expansion. New residents have found that towns like Holland Landing, Sutton, Keswick, East Gwillimbury, Tottenham, and Mourtt Albert are safe, friendly and family-oriented communities in which to bring up their families. You can still walk down any street in any one of those communities and recognize an acquaintance or a friendly face. These communities all boast strong municipal governments which provide excellent recreational facilities and activities that promote community interaction.
April 13, 1989

I am proud to say that the majority of people who do approach me are close acquaintances with whom I have worked in either a service organization or a voluntary group, cheered with at a hockey game, or even voted against at municipal meetings. Today, I am proud to demonstrate and represent the community spirit of my riding.
I know all my constituents will be looking to our Government to help maintain and foster the sense of community and sense of family so endeared to them, as I am sure it is to those in the rest of Canada.
Under the direction of the Prime Minister, I can assure my constituents that the Government will introduce legislation to create a child care program that addresses areas where it is required.
Despite the financial difficulties the Government faces, it will continue to provide assistance to families and the elderly, while directing greater assistance toward those with low incomes. We will be initiating legislation to reduce family violence, child abuse, and drug abuse. We will continue with criminal law reform which includes a review of the Young Offenders Act. We will also address the very sensitive issue of abortion.
Our approach to addressing the vast and diverse challenges in our changing Canadian society will be reflective of Canadian values. We have advised Canadians that we will be innovative in our approaches to handling the difficulties facing the Government.
Last November Canadians showed that they believe in the ways that we are trying to accomplish our objectives. In the Throne Speech we have shown that we will do everything in our power to ensure that the next generation will not blame the one before it.

speechtext:
I listened with great interest to my hon. friend on the Government benches as he discussed employment opportunities, post-secondary education, et cetera.
The Address-Mr. Manley
Yesterday I met with a scientific and educational society. Among other things, they were concerned about the loss of funding in the area of research, the loss of funding in the area of educational opportunities, and the brain drain that is occurring both in the public and private sectors. Our good Canadian minds are moving to the United States of America, to places such as NASA, a public facility where they are being offered large sums of money in order to work.
Those people cannot find jobs in Canada because of the Government's policies of cutbacks in the area of research. Over a period of time, research repays great dividends to the Canadian people. Whether it is geriatric research, agricultural research, or astrophysical research, we receive major returns in Canada from those dollars we put in. Yet we have seen a watering down of that in Canada over the last few years.
What will the Hon. Member do? Will he do more than talk about educational increases, employment, and the educational system, and press his Government to ensure that research funding is increased so that we can put an end to the brain drain from Canada and give our youth a future in our research community here in our own country?

Yesterday, I also met with representatives of that group. When I spoke to them I was encouraged. One of the ladies informed me that she had just received a research grant of over $100,000. This was a totally new grant from a totally new base. It was an industrial grant that came from the private sector, not the public sector.
When I mention innovative changes and changes coming from within the Government, we should be encouraging those types of changes. We have to ensure that the dollars we are spending are productive for us. If they are not productive, then they must be cut in order that we will have a more productive use of and value from our dollars.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to rise to speak in this debate with a sense that Canada stands today at some historic crossroads.

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Manley

It is a privilege to speak as the Official Opposition's critic for science and technology, since I am aware that science is very important for Canada if we want to compete in the global economy.

Canada is at an economic crossroads. We must soon decide how we will maintain our standard of living in light of the fact that we can no longer rely solely on the exploitation of our natural resources. The question we must ask ourselves is: Are we prepared to realize the potential of our far more important resource, our people?
The choice that Canadians must make is clear. We have to change our way of thinking, and our way of understanding economic development within the context of an environmental crisis. We have grown up believing that our natural resources are unlimited, that our wealth and standard of living is assured. This is not true.
As a people we have demonstrated determination, perseverance and ingenuity in conquering a massive continent, overcoming a hostile environment, and building a nation. We Canadians have pursued a path remarkable in its distinctiveness in the new world. History influences us deeply as we continually seek a renewal of the social compact that binds us together.
We are shaped by the strong influences of our two founding linguistic groups. However, we are also influenced in important ways by the special heritage of our aboriginal peoples, and by our more recently acquired multicultural diversity.
We forged a nation where logic dictated that none should exist. We built a new nation without denying our historic ties to our motherlands. We forged alliances, waged war against oppressors, and distinguished ourselves as international peace makers. We have set an example by sharing our wealth, although perhaps not enough, with those less fortunate, or those touched by destruction, disease, drought and famine.
Canada is a unique and special place. The world needs Canada, a middle power committed to freedom, to democracy, to peace; an open nation willing to criticize its friends while remaining loyal to historic alliances; an honest broker between superpowers; a nation able to understand the tensions and stresses of the world because it comprehends within its borders a richness of diversity and experience that mirrors the world at large.
The world needs Canada, and we have worked hard to create a place called Canada. Canada is more than a mere collection of regions, more than a nondescript adjunct to a North American superpower. Our single greatest achievement can be seen in the way we have related to each other.

Mr. Speaker, it is also my view that Canada is not only at an economic crossroads but at a constitutional one as well. Although the Prime Minister refuses to admit it, we are now going through a crisis. Canada's future is more in doubt now than it was in 1976 when Rene Levesque was elected.

Matters of human relations are not easy and they are always touched with fragility. There is no human relationship between individuals or between peoples that cannot be severed, no bond of friendship or loyalty that cannot be betrayed. Indeed, it is my view that there is no greater need in human society than the need for reconciliation.
That is why recent events have saddened me so much. I speak of the debate that has occurred in this Chamber and elsewhere on our Constitution. I speak of the legislative and public response of the Government of Quebec to the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada in the matter of minority language rights. First, I wish to address the matter of the Constitution and the process of constitutional reform.
For many years the sole exception to Canada's full legal status as a free democratic and independent nation was the necessity to seek the consent of the Parliament of the United Kingdom to any constitutional reform. The abolition of appeals to the Privy Council and the completion of the unification of British North America with the entry into Confederation of Newfoundland in 1949 almost completed the picture. Almost, but not quite. For more than 30 years after 1949, efforts to solve the difficulty of agreeing on how we as Canadians should amend our Constitution thwarted efforts to repatriate.
Agreement on an amending formula was reached in Victoria in 1971, only to be nullified by Robert Bourassa in a decision that I believe contributes directly to the present difficulties.
April 13, 1989

When the Supreme Court of Canada decided in 1981 that provincial consent was not required by law to amend the Constitution, the federal Government's will to repatriate the Constitution assumed greater importance. The fact that agreement on a new Constitution could not be achieved with the Government of Rene Levesque, a government whose purpose though thwarted by the will of the people, was the withdrawal of Quebec from Canada is hardly surprising. Rene Levesque did not line up with the other Premiers to sign the 1982 Constitution. That would have been like Ronald Reagan singing when "Irish Eyes are Smiling" with Daniel Ortega.
The people of Quebec did sign the Constitution. They signed with the pen of Pierre Trudeau. They signed with the pens of Jean Chretien and Andre Ouellet. They signed with the pens of all their federal Members of Parliament, men and women elected in Quebec by Quebecers, and with a mandate to affirm Canada, not to tear it down.
Is it necessary to even bother to seek the consent of the Government of Quebec? Indeed it is. Our federation recognizes the mutual sovereignty of federal and provincial levels of government, legislating within their own jurisdictions. Therefore, I believe that where this sovereignty is to be affected the consent of each sovereign government should be obtained. We should not, we cannot continue indefinitely without the sanction of the Government of Quebec for the 1982 reforms. But the Government of Pierre Trudeau was right, and courageous in so doing, to not permit the Separatist intentions of Rene Levesque to block constitutional reform. In a brave and modern departure from British constitutional tradition, our new made-in-Canada Constitution included a Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In addition, it included a clause that preserved the doctrine of the supremacy of Parliament by enabling laws to be enacted and enforced notwithstanding non-compliance with the Charter.
Pierre Trudeau and his Ministers did not favour including the notwithstanding clause. It was forced upon that government by Tory Premiers, such as Sterling Lyon of Manitoba. It was the price that had to be paid to have a Charter of Rights, as the former Solicitor General said in this House last week, the renegade Government of Rene Levesque responded immediately by invoking the notwithstanding clause in respect of all Quebec legislation. Despite the power to invoke notwithstanding, the
The Address-Mr. Manley
Canadian Charter of Rights establishes for all Canadians a concisely articulated statement of what we as a people believe should be the limits of power to be exercised by the Government. It also states clearly what we believe to be the overriding rights of the individual. A government invoking notwithstanding must now do so at its peril. We as a people have agreed on the Charter's formulation of basic rights. To suspend those rights must bring with it political consequences in a free society.
The Charter is not only a legal framework. The Charter is a standard, a measure of our freedom, of our respect for the liberties of the individual. It is for us all as parliamentarians, as law makers, as citizens, to point to the Charter, to hold it up, to assert its importance. It must grieve us all that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) would say that the Constitution, including the Charter of Rights, is not worth the paper it is written on.
I need not quote the comments of the Right Hon. Prime Minister in this House last Thursday, April 6, his attempt to rewrite history. It is sufficient to say that his denunciation of the 1982 Constitution was so overstated and hypocritical as to make one wonder at its audacity. The exaggeration on the part of our revisionist Prime Minister is obvious. Notwithstanding took nothing away from the Charter of Rights that was there before 1982. Before 1982 we had no written Charter. Parliament was absolutely supreme.
Mr. Diefenbaker's Bill of Rights, while a valiant and admirable effort, was a mere guide to statutory interpretation in its affirmation of rights. It did not limit Parliament's law-making ability. Of course, notwithstanding mitigated the effect of the Charter. But the Prime Minister is seriously misinformed when he tells the people of Canada that notwithstanding made the Constitution not worth the paper it is written on. Nothing was surrendered, only the gain was not as great as it might have been hoped. There is not one aspect of the Prime Minister's criticism of the 1982 Constitution that could not be applied with equal validity to his own efforts of constitutional reform in 1987, including the continuation of the notwithstanding clause. Why did he not attempt to remove the notwithstanding clause during the Meech Lake negotiations? If the 1982 Constitution is not worth the paper it is written on because it contains the notwithstanding clause, what value has been added to it by Meech Lake?

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Manley
The Prime Minister was not yet in this House when the 1982 Constitution was voted upon. But every Member of his present Cabinet who was a Member of this House at that time voted for the 1982 Constitution. The Prime Minister's attack last week is simply appalling, incredible, and indeed, disreputable. I would suggest that the example of public debate and consultation of the constitutional reform process in 1981-82 could well have been followed by the Prime Minister in his own effort.
The idea that the Meech Lake Accord was a seamless web, not amendable, nor even capable of meaningful debate by Canadians, is offensive.

I am convinced that the amendments proposed by the Liberal Party are essential and I fail to understand why the Prime Minister still refuses to consider them.

How is it that in a democratic society 11 men can lock themselves in a room all night, drink too much coffee, and change the basic contract whereby we live together as Canadians, and tell us that no, the other 25 million Canadians can have nothing to say about this? There were no women in that room at Meech Lake. There were no native people. There were no visible minorities. There were no representatives of the North. There was, in short, no respect for the need to have due process in the amendment of the Constitution.
The Prime Minister criticized the 1982 Constitution for having failed to enhance national unity. The divisions in this country provoked by the Prime Minister's effort at constitutional reform make the 1982 reform look like a children's birthday party.
Meech Lake is flawed and, tragically, it may be doomed. The Prime Minister knows it. The Prime Minister knows that the Premier of Quebec, by introducing Bill 178, may have sealed the fate of Meech Lake, and yet he will not say so. The Premier of Quebec, in claiming that notwithstanding would be unnecessary if Meech Lake were approved, is wrong since the Supreme Court decision was largely based upon the Quebec Charter, which is unaffected by Meech Lake. In this action the Premier has confirmed the greatest fears of
most Canadians about Meech Lake, and made its ratification exceedingly difficult. That is a great shame. It is a tragedy. I believe that Meech Lake should be ratified, but it must be further amended, because Canada needs to put an end to its pre-occupation with constitutional reform and language rights. Canada needs healing. Canada needs to focus its national will and build toward the future. Canada needs reconciliation, and therefore it needs national leaders who are reconcilers, healers.
Regrettably, the Prime Minister has failed in this task. He has let us all down by turning to partisan attacks when statesmanship was called for. I believe we can be sympathetic to the Premier's position as the leader of the only political entity in North America that has a Francophone majority.

We agree with Mr. Bourassa that the French language must be protected. Quebec must promote the French language.

But I would urge the Premier of Quebec, and indeed all the Premiers, to look again at the vision of a bilingual Canada. French language and culture is more endangered in a fortress Quebec, unilingual and isolated, than it is in a strong and bilingual Canada.
These are difficult and complex issues. I ventured to speak of them acknowledging my own inability to comprehend them fully, but believing as I do that Canada is a unique and special place, that Canadians are a people of considerable tolerance, and that the world needs Canada.
Canada is at a national crossroads. Unless we find our way here decisions about our economic crossroads may not long be ours to make together.
There are many other things, including the economic crossroads, that I would like to discuss, but my time has ended. Thus I will close on this final word. The world needs Canada. Canada more than ever needs leaders who are willing and able to be healers and reconcilers.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I attempted to have the Government make a commitment to research and development and to continued support of colleges and universities. Frankly, and I say this with total sincerity and generosity, I was not at all satisfied with the answers I received.
In the Speech from the Throne it was indicated that the Government would be following the recommendations of the National Advisory Board on Technology. I am wondering if my hon. friend, the Official Opposition critic, can give me his evaluation of the Government's performance to date in research, science and technology.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my hon. colleague for the question that he has put to me. It raises issues related to that economic crossroads that I was speaking about that Canada finds itself at.
Adjournment Debate
As I said in my remarks, we cannot any longer count on the sale of our natural resources to ensure our continued wealth and prosperity as a nation. What is critical for us is to go forward in new technologies, to train our people and to build on that key resource-our people. There are many numbers that show that Canada is lagging behind.
We know that the Prime Minister, before the 1984 election, promised to increase the ratio of gross expenditures on research and development to Gross Domestic Product, to 2.5 per cent, roughly double what it was at that time. Unfortunately, the record of the Government has been a failure in respect of that goal. In fact, by 1987 the gross expenditure ratio was 1.38 per cent compared to 1.37 per cent in 1984.
There are many other indicators that suggest that we are lagging behind in research and development. In our expenditure ratio we are last behind Finland, France, Germany, Japan, Norway, Sweden, the United Kingdom and the United States. Our R and D personnel per 100 in the labour force has barely moved since 1982, in spite of the importance of having these people employed and doing new work.
According to the last year for which there are statistics, 1986, there were eight per thousand R and D personnel in Canada. France has 11.4. Japan has 12.9. The Netherlands has 10.7. Switzerland has 13.9. It is crucial that we begin to find ways to increase our concentration in science and technology, engineering and research. We have to take advantage of our intelligent population, of our vast expanse of educational infrastructure, to ensure that Canada can build the means to compete in the modern era.
Our resources will only last so long. Indeed, when one considers the recent developments in nuclear physics, one wonders whether a major resource, that of petroleum, is going to continue to be a source of earnings for us if the discoveries in nuclear fusion prove to be as exciting as they promise.
We have to deal with these items. We need to deal with them in a way that really takes into account the importance for the future of these types of expenditures, notwithstanding the level of the Government's deficit. Deficits need to be taken into account in deciding how any government money is going to be spent. Spending on research, on education and on our people is essential, otherwise our deficits in the future will only grow. Our economic prospects for the future depend on our ability to grow in science, engineering and technology.

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Malepart

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the graciousness you have shown me. My answer to the question is that where minority rights are not protected by any Government, it is indeed in my opinion the majority who is threatened. Each of us who are in today's majority must know that our own rights are only as safe as those of the weakest person in our society.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on the Speech from the Throne. I prepared a long speech to explain that first of all, the Throne Speech contains a lot of "rehashed stuff" and that the
Government wanted to reduce the deficit but did the exact opposite during its first four years in power.
Second, when the Throne Speech refers to social programs, we know the Government has already cut $13 billion in funding.
However, I think I would rather skip my prepared speech and try to explain, speaking as a Quebecer and speaking to all Hon. Members and to English Canada, what it means to be a Francophone Quebecer in this bilingual country of ours where everyone dreams of being bilingual.
First of all, bilingualism is for Francophones and unilingualism, for Anglophones. An Anglophone in the House of Commons can show off his few words of French and say: Bonjour monsieur, fa va bien? But a Francophone has to be fully bilingual.
I think it is important for all Members of this House to realize how the population of Quebec is made up. Twenty per cent are Quebecers but they are Canadians first and Quebecers second. They live in the riding or Mount Royal, in Westmount. They are Anglophones. They believe in Canada first, and Quebec second. Another 20 per cent are at the opposite end of the spectrum. They are separatists, want nothing to do with Canada and are in a hurry to get out of Confederation. The remaining 60 per cent, and that includes me, are Quebecers first and Canadians second, and during the last referendum... Mr. Trudeau was able to patriate the Constitution thanks to the results of the referendum in Quebec. With other Francophones, I fought the separatists. I wasn't in the riding of Mount Royal then. I fought against Charron and Burns and all those pillars of the PQ establishment. Because of those results, even when no decision was forthcoming from the National Assembly, either from Fiberal or PQ members, there was an unwillingness to start the patriation process.
At the time I worked very hard because I was convinced that English Canada, my own colleagues and other Members would say: Yes, stay in Canada, we will try to understand. However, when I consider the reactions to Meech Fake, I get the impression that English Canada still doesn't understand. When I listen to comments on Bill 178, and I hear my English-speaking friends from Quebec complain, and then when I look at how Francophones in other provinces are treated-they are in a disaster area and Quebec's Anglophones are the best protected minority in the whole world!
April 13, 1989

We must realize that 60 per cent of the Francophones in Quebec are Quebecers first and Canadians second, but that 60 per cent said yes to Canada. However, the way things are now, I think if there was another referendum, I would work for the other side. Sometimes I wonder, when I hear some of the Provincial Premiers talk about Meech Lake, what Quebec has to gain from being associated with these people. We would be better off with the Americans. We might get more respect and be better understood.
The minority language at risk in this country is not English, according to D'Iberville Fortier, the Official Languages Commissioner, it is French. French is at risk in the other provinces, but can you imagine that even in the very heartland, as Mr. Trudeau said, of the French fact, even in Quebec the French community is at risk. Mr. Bourassa had no choice. I agree. He had no choice but to use the notwithstanding clause to protect the French fact. I am not saying that signs are the best way to protect the French fact, but Quebec must be able to keep some tools. It cannot leave it up to the Parliament of Canada to protect the French fact in Quebec, because history has shown that Canada has not protected French in Quebec.
At one time there were more English radio stations than French networks accredited by the CRTC in Quebec.
In the 1982 Constitution, Mr. Trudeau, although he did not support the idea, agreed to let the Canada Clause prevail in Quebec and the universal clause prevail in the other provinces with respect to the language of education. Although he did not support the idea because he was in favour of free choice, he knew perfectly well that his Members would not accept that, and perhaps if his initial proposal had been successful, it would have caused chaos in Quebec with respect to the language of education. In immigration matters, there again, Quebec and only the Parliament of Quebec can afford the province the protection it needs, and as Mr. Bourassa said: We cannot transfer the authority to protect the French fact in Quebec to another Parliament whose members belong mostly to the majority.
The same applies to the language of education and the same applies to culture.
Mr. Speaker, in Quebec our most effective tool is the language of work. I was a Member in Quebec City when the Government passed Bill 22. I agree a number of mistakes were made in Bill 22 and what happened in the
The Address-Mr. Malepart
area of language tests was unacceptable. But Bill 101 was the legislation that kept the peace in Quebec. It enforced while respecting the rights of the anglophone community, rights of employers and unions alike, and there were no problems.
There was agreement in Ottawa to replace the Quebec clause with the Canada clause. Since we had decided to remain in Canada, it was right that anyone in Canada who had been schooled in English and was transferred to Quebec could have his or her children educated in English. But those who come from other countries to Quebec would have to go to French school and integrate. Language of work may be the area where the Bourassa Government has not done enough to promote the French fact, but I must tell you in all honesty that I do not think that my leader's speech and the Prime Minister's recent speech on the Constitution have done a lot to advance Canadian unity. All that they achieved was to force us Quebecois and the Premier of Quebec to oppose any change to the notwithstanding clause. And you know that a minority which feels threatened often is obliged to cling to symbols.
The question of unilingual French signs is a symbol and that is not what will save our language. But unfortunately, what Alliance Quebec and others are doing about Meech Lake just repels the majority of Quebecois, who at first were in favour of multilingual signs and who have had to take a harder line against them and want to maintain unilingual signs. I now wonder whether it would be better for the provinces to reject Meech Lake, because the way things are going, if my children some day want to say yes to independence, it would be preferable for English Canada to say no to Quebec's joining the Constitution, because then we could say that the first time, the Constitution was imposed and the second time, English Canada rejected us. We could go to the United Nations and say that we were separating, that we had nothing to do with that country, that we had tried everything.
I am talking to you as I would to an ordinary citizen. My way of talking may not be correct, but I think that I am expressing here the opinion of a majority of Francophone Quebecers who for years and years had to submit and they do not want to anymore. We want to have our own place. We want to have our place and the assurance that Quebec will be French, that my children will continue to want to work in French and I would hope that I can work only in French in Canada and be accepted and I would hope that my children can continue

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Malepart
to do the same, that they will not need to think of separating.
But I say to all those who are afraid of Meech Lake, who are afraid of the distinct society, that it is necessary if they really want Canadian unity and if they want Quebec to remain in Canada. I often had conversations with Mr. Trudeau. I understand him, his style; he does not need the distinct society. He can go anywhere in the world and that is fine.
But such is not the case for each man and woman in Quebec. Before the people of Quebec can feel at ease and at home in this country.. . because a visit to Ottawa will not convince them that they are in their own country. Some of the commissionaires do not speak a word of French, and some of the restaurant waiters and waitresses do not speak a word of French, so better not try to tell the people of Lac-Saint-Jean that this beautiful country is bilingual. And in the national capital to boot! If you go to Winnipeg, Edmonton or even further west people over there wonder what Francophones eat in winter! Quebecers want to remain in Canada, but they want the Constitution to make English Canada accept them as they are. We fought against separatism in Quebec because at the time-I was right here-Pierre Elliott Trudeau assured us that the Constitution would be changed and that Quebec would be understood. Unfortunately, I must say that Pierre Elliott Trudeau and other English-speaking Canadians still do not understand Quebec's majority as it is. And if in two or three years. . . Perhaps the Meech Lake Accord is dead right now because of the stubborness of two or three provinces.
Honestly, Quebecers will not insist all that much on having Meech Lake, but Canada will lose Quebec because we can continue to function. Legally we belong to the Constitution and the day we decide to pull out we will be able to do so politically because we have always sought to survive on our own and not depend on others. But English Canada stands to lose more if it continues to be inflexible and refuses to acknowledge the distinct character. People say: We want Quebec in Confederation, we want Quebec to promote the French fact, but every time Quebec does something to protect the French fact it becomes the target of criticism.
I spoke against Bill 178 because I did not agree when Mr. Bourassa granted what is called multilingual signs inside stores.
I can understand that English-speaking people were "offended", because Mr. Bourassa was wrong when he said: Listen, outside the stores, I cannot authorize the use of signs in languages other than English, because the ban does not apply only to English signs, but also to Chinese, Japanese, Polish, and other languages. However, I cannot stop you from using English signs inside your establishments. I can relate to the English-speaking people who were "offended" by Mr. Bourassa's behaviour. He should have said: As a result ot the Supreme Court decision... But we must not forget that, it was as a result of the Supreme Court decision which acknowledged that French was being threatened in the province of Quebec, that the Quebec provincial government used the notwithstanding clause which had been included in the Constitution by a Liberal government. So, Quebec cannot be accused of stealing anything, or of inventing a new strategy.
Mr. Speaker, I know that my time is up. I do hope that the people in English Canada, and maybe even some politicians, whether they be Conservative, New-Demo-crat, or Liberal, who proclaim out loud that they want Quebec in the Constitution while in fact hiding their true feelings, will come to see, after hearing my speech, the other side of the coin, the point of view of a Quebecer, an ordinary French-speaking citizen of Quebec. And I think that I speak for 60 per cent of all French-speaking Quebecers who agree with me.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all, when someone has leadership, the Leader of the Opposition does not move things forward; the Conservative Prime Minister does. If he had backbone, if he had courage, he would have moved things forward. I think that Pierre Elliott Trudeau could be blamed for a lot of things, but he always had the courage of his convictions. You could be for him or against him, but you respected that man because he was capable. If you have influence with your Prime Minister, if he is a Conservative Prime Minister with courage, he will take charge and lead proceedings in the House and not let the Opposition guide him. Otherwise, it would be better for him to resign and turn power over to others.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to rise today and join in the debate on the Throne Speech. I appreciate that the Throne Speech touches on many issues, economic and social.
In my capacity as Minister of Justice, I want to address the justice matters referred to in the Throne Speech, one briefly, and another in some depth. The part I wish
The Address-Mr. Lewis
to address briefly is that comment in the Speech from the Throne:
My government will introduce further legislation to reform
Canada's legal system and sentencing practices.
There have been a number of reports and studies to look into the question of criminal sentencing. There is the Canadian Sentencing Commission's Report and the Report of the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General which was entitled "Taking Responsibility". I intend to work to determine the status of the various reports, to establish some focus and, from there, put together with my Cabinet colleagues a Government initiative on sentencing which will focus on the need to address the unwarranted disparities which occur in sentences in Canada.
Specifically today, I want to refer to the reference in the Speech from the Throne which states:
This will require a review of the current Young Offenders Act in
order to ensure that it better protects the rights of society while
advancing the rehabilitation of young offenders.
In the time available to me I want to examine the history of the Young Offenders Act, to review the difficulties, whether they are real or imagined, and to stake out our position as a Government and review the proposed course of action.
The House will know that the Juvenile Delinquents Act which governed juvenile justice from 1908 to 1984 had become ineffective and inappropriate. The Juvenile Delinquents Act was based on one clear and simple goal, and that was that juvenile offenders should be treated not as criminals but as children needing encouragement, assistance and guidance. Quite frankly, it became out of date.
It was revised by the previous Government and because of some criticisms I think it is fair that we review those briefly.
First, although the police, the courts and social welfare institutions were expected to act in the best interests of the child there was no expressed recognition in the legislation of the principle of protection of society. There was an imbalance between the interests of individual juveniles and the interests of society.
It stated that adolescents should be responsible for their actions and should be held criminally accountable if guilty of offences. The simple transfer of adolescents to the authority of child welfare authorities was not appropriate.

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Lewis
Closed courts denied the public and the media access. The age level at which juvenile delinquents would become subject to the adult court system varied from province to province. Finally, young people were denied fundamental rights which were enjoyed by adults.
The Act was passed by the previous Government and I would say at this point that it had all-Party support. Its two main objectives are to ensure protection of the public and to promote the rehabilitation of young people wherever possible. It is based upon four key principles which attempt to strike that balance between the needs of young people and the interests of society. The first principle is that young people are responsible for their behavior and should be held accountable in a manner appropriate to their age and maturity. Second, society has a right to protection from illegal behavior and a responsibility to prevent criminal conduct by young people as well as an obligation to promote their rehabilitation. Third, young people have special needs because of their varying levels of development and maturity. The fourth principle is that young people, if they are to be held accountable, are entitled to the same rights as adults, to due process of law and fair and equal treatment in accordance with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
To achieve the balance that the Young Offenders Act seeks, young people may require not only supervision, discipline and control but also guidance and assistance. For that reason, the Act provides alternative measures to the formal court process or perhaps no measures at all if the solution is consistent with the protection of society. In addition, the Act recognizes the responsibility of parents for the care and supervision of their children.
I should as an aside point out that I have discussed this with various officials at different levels and I was struck by the comment of one Crown Attorney who said to me that they see many more parents than they did under the Juvenile Delinquents Act because the Young Offenders Act puts an onus on the parents to be responsible for their children and they are seeing more parents in court. I think that is helpful.
The Act also says that young offenders should be removed from parental supervision only when that continued parental supervision is inappropriate. Parents will be encouraged and, if necessary, required to take an active part in proceedings that involve their children.
The Young Offenders Act is criminal law but it is different from the criminal law that applies to adults because of the doctrine of special needs. That doctrine says that the special needs of a young offender must be taken into account in determining the extent and the nature of the criminal law as distinct from or concurrent with interventions by the youth's family and by other systems such as child welfare, education or health.
As I mentioned a minute ago, when the Young Offenders Act was passed, it had broad parliamentary support. This is an issue that does cut across Party lines because there is no fundamental partisan or philosophical differences regarding young offenders. We all want to achieve that balance between protecting public property and persons and rehabilitating young people. We do not want young people to make one mistake and then find that that is just the first of many.
It is fair to say that the implementation process was difficult, especially the implementation of a maximum age of 17 years inclusive. I do not think anyone should be surprised to find that, when replacing a law such as the Juvenile Delinquents Act which had been in existence for 74 years, there were some implementation problems.
In 1985, when the experience of the first year's implementation showed that there were some problems and some concerns, our Government, under the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty), consulted with the territories and the provinces and identified specific problems which were based on the legislation itself. Amendments were passed to address these problems. They did not affect the fundamental principle, but they worked out a lot of the glitches.
The Act has been in force for four years now, and what has happened? What is the real experience of the Act as opposed to a few isolated and perhaps sensationalized incidents? I think Hon. Members will be surprised by some of the comments I will make, because I will talk about the actual experience across Canada.
Notwithstanding the wide range of dispositions available in the legislation and the principle of least interference, it appears that more young people are being sent into custody. Second, the bulk of young offenders commit property-related offences. That comprises about two-thirds of the charges laid. We are finding that a significant number of young offenders enter and exit the system only once.
April 13, 1989

Only 9 per cent of the offences recorded under the Young Offenders Act are violent offences, and only a minute proportion of those refer to the charge of murder, less than one-twentieth of 1 per cent. Probation is the most common disposition rendered, although there is compensation, community work and similar orders. Detention for treatment is rarely ordered as a disposition.
That is the experience. What are the criticisms? It is interesting to note that some say that the Act is too tough and some say that it is too lenient. The major criticisms have been the treatment order provisions which require the consent of the young person, the fact that children under 12 are excluded from the reach of the criminal law, the sufficiency of the maximum sentence, especially for murder, and the difficulty of transfers to adult court for serious crimes because of the necessity to prove under Section 16 of the Act that the transfer is in the interests of society and, and I think the difficult world is "and", having regard to the needs of the young person. The last criticism is the increasing proportion of young persons being incarcerated.
We have identified these areas in consultation with the provinces and the territories, and we looked at areas where there was a consensus that action had to be taken. In January 1989, all the jurisdictions involved agreed that on an expedited basis the focus of the study should be narrowed to the transfer provisions and dispositions for youth who murder.
We expect that this review will be completed shortly. I have asked that the results be available for discussion at an early meeting of provincial Ministers concerned with juvenile justice, and I can assure Hon. Members that we will act if we can find some consensus. We are looking toward a meeting with the provincial Attorneys General which I believe is in early June in Prince Edward Island.
I want to make one point, if I may, vis-a-vis the current incidents that have been reported in the media. Many of them have occurred in the Province of Ontario. There has been a suggestion that these alleged deficiencies are as a result of the Young Offenders Act. I want to suggest that they may be the result of administrative difficulties rather than deficiencies in the Act.
The Address-Mr. Lewis
To his credit, the Minister of Community and Social Services in Ontario, the Hon. John Sweeney, has ordered an investigation into possible administrative difficulties, and I have offered the co-operation of my Department in assisting him in those studies. If we can separate the administrative difficulties from those two items that I referred to, the transfer provisions and especially the sentence for the crime of murder, it would be helpful to try to understand who has the responsibility for what.
I would also point out that in the past the federal Government has cost-shared the delivery of juvenile justice services with the provinces and the territories. The original agreement was to cost-share the first five years and review the actual experience. That review is not completed yet, but I recently announced a one-year extension of the Young Offenders System Development Contribution Program and the Young Offenders Program Development Contribution Program in an effort to maintain that joint responsibility. We are cost-sharing to the tune of some $160 million per annum, and that will continue until we are able to reach some new agreements.
I just want to say in closing that I do not think it will ever be easy to draft a law for young people that will exactly suit every province in this vast country. There are different thoughts as to how young people should be treated. That is the way we are. It will never be easy to draft laws that balance protection of person and property with our concern that we rehabilitate young people so they are an asset to society and not a liability to society and themselves. That is the challenge we face.
We are attempting to meet that challenge in a nonpartisan way. It is evident the rehabilitation of young people, the effective treatment of them and the protection of personal property, cut across Party lines.
I am here to take part in the Throne Speech debate specifically in order to show exactly where the Government of Canada is headed in respect to any amendments vis-a-vis this very important law.

speechtext:
I want to take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister on his appointment as Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and to commend him on the approach he is taking on the very difficult and sensitive question of possible amendments to the Young Offenders Act. As one who was involved in

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Lewis
the drafting of the legislation and saw it through the Justice Committee, we as New Democrats recognize there have been difficulties. In some jurisdictions, too many people are being incarcerated. In others, we recognize there is a problem of two extremes in the area of murder. The community does recognize a concern that there is a disposition of three years in the case of youth court, or a life sentence with a minimum of 25 years if the young person is transferred to adult court. We want to look at some means of reducing that wide disparity in sentencing and give greater options to the judges. I want to offer my co-operation and that of my colleagues in trying to arrive at an equitable resolution of this difficult question.
In the 1986 Speech from the Throne, the Government promised amendments to the Canadian Human Rights Act. A number of concerns were expressed in this area. In the Speech from the Throne tabled on April 3 of this year, there was no reference whatsoever to changes to the Canadian Human Rights Act. In the annual report of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, serious concerns were expressed about the failure of the Government to bring forward long overdue amendments to the Canadian Human Rights Act. These amendments are in the areas of equal pay for work of equal value; reasonable accommodation, which affects religious minorities and the disabled; reporting directly to Parliament; and also expanding the prohibited grounds of discrimination to include political belief and sexual orientation.
On the question of sexual orientation, the Government promised over three years ago, and I quote from the Government's response to the Equality Rights Report:
The Government will take whatever measures are necessary to ensure that sexual orientation is a prohibited ground of discrimination in relation to all areas of federal jurisdiction.
Lesbians and gay men continue to be victims of discrimination. They are fired from their jobs and denied access to housing and services. They are subject to harassment, violence and even death, as we have recently seen in Montreal. My question for the Minister is, does the Government stand behind the promise that was made three years ago to ensure that sexual orientation is a prohibited ground of discrimination in relation to all areas of federal jurisdiction?
When will the Government be bringing forward the long-overdue amendments to the Canadian Human Rights Act which have been promised for some time? Will it be in this session?

I appreciate my hon. colleague's kind comments. I welcome his offer of assistance with respect to amendments to the Young Offenders Act.
We have been trying to balance our agenda vis-a-vis items such as the Young Offenders Act and other initiatives in the justice field. I am thinking in terms of sentencing, firearms legislation and abortion. The matter of amendments to the Human Rights Act are on the agenda. We are reviewing the human rights issues my hon. friend raised. We are looking at the current annual report which raised a number of new issues. We will be putting these issues together in the context of our legislative program.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the Minister for taking the initiative and putting forward in the Throne Speech that amendments to the Young Offenders Act will be put into place. However, I did not hear the Minister today reassure Members opposite that some measures will be put into place. The Minister said that 9 per cent of the crimes committed are violent crimes. He said he has real experience. I have worked on amendments to the Young Offenders Act. I have received the same kind of letters the Hon. Minister has received. If he is reading those letters, he will see the Canadian public expressing a need for change. Violent crimes such as murder need to be addressed.
Would the Minister say he will take positive steps and not side-step the issue? Will the Minister reassure this House that when the charge is murder and the young offender is over 14 years of age, that young offender will be transferred to adult court? Will the Minister also reassure this House he will reflect what the Canadian public wants, a maximum sentence to be increased from three years to five years less a day? Will the Minister reassure us that those will be the steps he will take after he meets with his colleagues in Prince Edward Island?

I want to assure my hon. colleague that I read as many letters as I can to get a flavour of what people are thinking. That was my practice as a Member of Parliament and I have continued it as a Minister. I would state unequivocally that we are addressing the issue. Through the context of federal-provincial
April 13, 1989

meetings we are attempting to see if a problem in one province is a problem shared by the other provinces and Territories.
Our discussions have been narrowed down to two issues: (a) the transfer provisions which, when they are applied, do provide for a longer sentence than three years; and (b) the sentence for murder. I have given my undertaking to address that issue. I am doing everything I can from the standpoint of the federal Government. There was a consensus among all parties involved that those were the issues to be studied. I am pushing to get a resolution and consensus that I hope will be forthcoming in June. If we get that consensus, I will have some time in the summer to go back to my cabinet colleagues and see what amendments we can draft.

I appreciate the courtesy of the House in granting me time for this question. I was a member of the Justice Committee that dealt with the Young Offenders Act. I appreciate the Minister's observation that more and more parents are involved in court proceedings. That gives us encouragement that they are becoming more involved in their children's lives. I know there are many parents across Canada who have incorrigible children, and it is not the fault of the parents. It is simply that the children are incorrigible.
At the time we were dealing with the legislation and dealing with the clause that outlines the purposes of the Bill, and there were approximately eight of them. The last one, the eighth, was listed as working with the parents or giving parental responsibility for the conduct of the children.
The then Solicitor General, the Member for York Centre, found it impossible to accommodate a simple change that would have put clause No. 8 to clause No. 1. This would have given more direct focus to parental responsibility. I do not believe that it was a monumental request to ask for that type of change of simply moving the order of priorities. I believe it was a mistake not to do that.
The Address-Mr. Schneider
I would ask the Minister, given the fact that the legislation already gives focus to that and the fact that parents seem to have found help in the Young Offenders legislation in working with their children, if he would assure us that in the amendments to come there will be an even greater focus on parental accountability and parents' right to work with the courts to ensure that young offenders are held accountable?

It is interesting that the one aside I used in my prepared text was to speak of a Crown Attorney who told me that they were seeing more parents coming to court. It is partly a policing matter and partly more effective work by the provinces in looking for new ways of dealing with rehabilitation.
I can say to my hon. friend that I do not believe it has been the thrust of a lot of demands by various provinces and the Territories for an amendment which would rearrange the principles and perhaps give a higher priority, if in fact listing does give a priority to the comment my hon. friend makes, but I will take it under advisement.
