speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I bring you greetings from the unofficial rump of the Government. Although we are only 18 strong, we represent significant strength and support for our fellow members on your right. Our comfort level is high as our view is much better from here than is theirs.
It is an honour and privilege for me to rise in the House and take part in the Throne Speech debate. It is certainly a source of great pride being the first Member from Regina to be elected to the Government in 26 years, especially coming during such an historic election campaign.
On November 21, Canadians decided which direction the country would take, not only for the next four years but into the 21st Century. Canadians chose a Government with a vision for the future and rejected the closed isolationist view of Canada put forward by the opposition parties.

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Schneider
Canadians elected a Government committed to building a stronger economy so that we can afford to maintain the type of caring and compassionate society that we now enjoy. We are committed to the enhancement and protection of our environment. We remain committed to the promotion of national unity, not only between English and French, but among all peoples who make up the multicultural mosaic of Canada.
Canadians correctly believed that the Progressive Conservative Party possessed the type of leader it takes to steer our country through difficult times. They saw a leader who had overcome adversity and not lost sight of his dream to build a better Canada, a leader with the integrity, determination and courage to fight and win an election against two opposition parties. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) showed us what it takes to move this country forward. Canadians chose a leader and a Party capable of adapting to the future.
My Leader and my Party are positive about the future of this country. That is why the Speech from the Throne confidently states our objectives and commitments. Unlike some opposition Members, I know that Canada remains a sovereign nation. As Canadians, we would not have it any other way.
We have entered into a trading agreement with the United States that will make Canada stronger and more competitive, and it is this strength that nurtures our sovereignty. I ask Members opposite to join with the Conservatives and the Ontario Liberals in supporting the Free Trade Agreement. It is time to stop fighting the election and get on with building a better Canada. Even the Liberals must realize that blaming every sparrow that falls on the Free Trade Agreement is divisive and counterproductive for this great country that we all share. Surely that is not their objective.
By accepting free trade we have acknowledged the need to compete in a global market-place. This is not a new idea to those of us from the prairies. Saskatchewan farmers have always competed internationally, and they have and will continue to be successful because they are extremely good at what they do.
It is not freer trade that hurts the farmer; it is protectionism and unfair trading practices. It is also protectionism which hurts the development of manufacturing and secondary processing in Saskatchewan and in Canada.
Of course, I have no illusions about members of the New Democratic Party's approach to free trade, or anything else for that matter. As if their ideological approach to the future were not already made clear enough during the election, the leader of the NDP restated it on April 7 in this House when he said: "We are going to oppose with determined vigour every Bill that flows out of this Throne Speech and every Budget item that will come in the weeks ahead", for no specific reason other than opposition.
It does not matter what will come from the Throne Speech or the Budget, members of the New Democratic Party already know they must be against it. Perhaps things will change in November, but I rather doubt it. Members of the NDP will oppose any new initiative. It is not surprising they oppose the Government's new labour force strategy.
As was stated earlier in the House today, it is because the NDP is an old Party with old socialist ideas that even socialist countries today are rejecting them. I am sure that the additional $350 million for job training under Section 26 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, enough to train an addition 60,000 Canadians, will be opposed. It is of interest to note how the New Democratic Party can selectively make use of information to suit its purposes in opposition.
In the House, Members of that Party have been known not only to criticize actions of the federal Government, but also be critical of members of provincial Governments who are unable to defend themselves here.
Criticism was levelled the other day at the Saskatchewan Conservatives. The comparison was made that while under an NDP Government in Saskatchewan, Saskatchewan enjoyed a balanced budget, more social programs and lower taxes. Parts of the statement are true, while other parts are based on a jaundiced form of judgment.
This criticism is not honest in that it makes no reference to the fact that at the time the provincial Conservatives took office, world oil, uranium, and potash prices plummeted. As we all know, Saskatchewan has been victimized by drought. The recession caused the Government of Saskatchewan to invest in job creation programs and technology investment, not the least of which is an $850 million investment in Canada's first heavy oil upgrader in Regina.
April 13, 1989

The Address-Mr. Schneider
At that time the greatest tragedy attributable to the NDP Government in Saskatchewan was that when the provincial Conservatives took office in 1982, the cupboard of the provincial heritage fund was bare. The mice had taken it all. The explanation was that 50 per cent of Saskatchewan's potash industry was to be nationalized for the benefit of future generations. Members of the Saskatchewan NDP went down to New York for a loan. How can a U.S. loan, borrowed when the dollar was in the mid-80 cent range and attempted to be repaid when the dollar was in the mid-70 cent range, benefit Saskatchewan's future generations? Shortly after, world potash prices fell. Instead of owning an asset, Saskatchewan residents found themselves as the owners of a liability.
During the same period, the Alberta Conservatives chose to tax the mining of Alberta resources and not socialize them under the pretext of ownership. History shows the Alberta approach to have been a monumentally better decision for the average Albertan.
The Alberta Heritage Trust Fund has been used to allow Alberta municipalities to pay off large amounts of debt, and to pay for a large portion of the light rail transit systems in Edmonton and Calgary. As well, there is a long list for the average Albertan to benefit from.
No, Mr. Speaker, Members of the NDP do not possess a better way. They have no magic formula. A provincial NDP cabinet minister once conveyed to me a most honest statement. He said words to the effect that he wished people would stop asking the Government to do things for them. He went on to say that what people do not realize is that the more a Government is involved in our lives, the more of our freedoms we stand to lose. This was an honest admission that he detested his Party's basic philosophy. This man has since retired and I have not heard from him politically since. No wonder.
I want no part of a socialist entrapment. Socialists thrive on the takeover of the body; socialists excel at the takeover of the mind. That is the illness of socialism, and I want no part of it. My grandparents came to this country to be free people and it is under this Conservative Government that we will all continue to be free.
We cannot spend our time trying to please the NDP. We must continue to work for the people of Canada. They are the ones for whom we are all here. That is why the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) has announced her intention to revise the maternity, parental and sickness benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Currently, maternity benefits are available to natural mothers only for a period of 15 weeks. With these new changes a total of 30 weeks will be available. Parental benefits will soon be accessible to fathers as well as mothers, whether they be natural or adoptive parents. This will bring the Act in line with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It is this kind of action that Canadians want and expect from the Government. So they should.
By developing a human resources development strategy the Government is investing in our strongest asset, our people. We are helping people adapt to a changing environment. It is the type of initiative that will prepare Canadians for the challenges that lie ahead. It is a recognition by this Government that it has a major role to play in maintaining the competitiveness of Canadians, and that skill development is crucial to competitiveness. That is why we remain committed to our initiatives in literacy, education, training and retraining. Our workforce, especially our youth, must meet the requirements of a modern economy. Through the expansion of labour force programs to encourage the continual upgrading of skills, we will maintain a stronger productive workforce, world class and world competitive. These are initiatives aimed at the average Canadian, designed to ensure that the average Canadian will benefit fully from a Canadian economy prepared for the pressures of the new global reality.
As we have in the past, we will ensure that Canada's first Canadians continue to make progress toward economic equality. In 1988-89, some 15,000 native people will receive close to $130 million in federal assistance for post-secondary education. I am confident that the Budget will continue to increase in the future, as it has over the past two years.
It is necessary to make sure that all Canadians share in the benefits of economic success, no matter what part of Canada they live in. That is why we remain committed to regional development throughout the country. The

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Schneider
Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced that the regional economic diversification programs will continue to be funded for an additional five years, to support the efforts of Canadians in expanding beyond our traditional areas of strength. I know that in Saskatchewan we are taking advantage of the federal support to bring to life the ideas that lie at the root of all new economic expansions. We have always been proud of the ingenuity and the pioneering spirit which built our province. We are using those same qualities today to create new industries and therefore new opportunity. I know that the people of Saskatchewan can succeed in their effort to build a stronger and more vibrant economy. I am pleased to be part of the federal Government that will continue to work with us as we strive to achieve our goal.
Yet, as we work to create the kind of rich, varied economy that will bring a better life for all Canadians, there is a burden we must carry that impedes our progress. That burden is the massive national debt. There are those who would try to convince us that the debt is not a serious matter, that other priorities must come first, as if the debt did not intrude on every area of Government decision making. The fact is, the debt is slowly strangling our ability to deal effectively with the needs of Canadians.
It is not the kind of problem that can be casually cast aside and forgotten about. We must deal with it now. Despite our progress over the last four years in reducing the yearly deficits by some $10 billion more is required. I am afraid much more.
The debt is so large that it is almost beyond comprehension. The numbers have been repeated so often that they are becoming meaningless. Surely, though, when we reach the point that 31 cents out of every dollar the Government spends goes to servicing the debt it is time to act decisively and to act together.
Arguments are tossed back and forth as to who is to blame for the state we find ourselves in today. But that is seemingly insignificant. We must either begin to solve the problem or soon control will be lost. And when I say we, I again urge the support of the opposition Parties. I invite real criticism but please do not bother me with useless rhetorical opposition. The debt is our problem. It is Canada's problem. Given the proper attitude, it can be addressed.
Regrettably, debt problems are not new to the agricultural sector in Saskatchewan. The combination of drought and the international agricultural trade war have taken a heavy toll. But the Progressive Conservative Government has been there to support our farmers and have thus supported our consumers. There may have only been a brief mention about farmers in the Throne Speech, but this is a Government that believes in actions not words.
Between 1984 and August of 1988, this federal Government provided $10.3 billion in agricultural benefits to farmers. We have responded to the needs of farmers in the past and we will continue to do so. The Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program will put approximately $850 million into the pockets of Canadian agricultural producers. The assistance to farmers is much more than drought relief. We are active in developing the rural infrastructure through the Rural Water Development Program. The $500,000 capital gains exemption for farmers and the farm fuel tax rebate are initiatives which highlight our ongoing support for the farmer. We have worked tirelessly on behalf of the agricultural community on the international scene. Through our involvement in the Cairns Group we have lobbied for the kind of international trading rules that will allow our farmers to develop their competitive advantage. In Saskatchewan we have some of the best agricultural producers in the world. Our Government will continue to support them through concrete actions as they have in the past.
Mr. Speaker, our international role is not limited to economic matters. We will continue, as we have in the past, to take a strong stand in defence of human rights. Only the constant vigil of the free nations of the world and the weight of world public opinion can bring true freedom to the victims of oppression. In many parts of the world people suffer under the oppression of war. Canada remains committed to working with the United Nations as peacekeepers to help end this suffering, to do our best to relieve the pain of famine and other natural disasters.
We have a role to play in encouraging East-West co-operation while remembering that we are firmly committed to our allies in NATO. It is important to remember our historical ties with Western Europe, especially now when there is so much hope for change in the Soviet Union. We must do what we can to encourage these positive developments, but not at the expense of losing touch with the real situation. There is a long road to travel before the Soviet Union becomes a truly free society. Until that time we must remain vigilant.
April 13, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I have only mentioned a few of the areas in which the Government can act over the next four years. Judging from our past record, I am sure we will accomplish a great deal in many other areas as well. The agenda of the government is clear and confident. Our resolve is firm. I believe we will continue to move this country forward by working in the national interest.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Winnipeg Transcona (Mr. Blaikie) on questions and comments.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would like to begin by congratulating the Hon. Member for Regina-Wascana (Mr. Schneider) on his speech, but my congratulations end there. The Member spent a great deal of time talking about the NDR We are grateful for the attention but it certainly is an indication to us who the Hon. Member regards as the force to be reckoned with in Regina and Saskatchewan. The Hon. Member, we know, is an old partisan of Saskatchewan politics, being a former mayor of Regina, if I remember correctly.
He mentioned that this is the first time in 26 years the people of Regina had elected a Conservative and, after listening to his speech, my colleagues and 1 are comforted to know this is something that will indeed be something which will only happen every 26 years. The people of Regina are entitled to make this mistake four times a century. It is not something they will do often, especially since the Hon. Member appears to be doing his best to ensure that that tradition will be upheld by distorting the political tradition which the NDP represents and which the Saskatchewan people hold dear.
I hope the Hon. Member goes on ranting and raving the way he did this afternoon, because I am sure this is the kind of thing which will only ensure that very shortly in the Province of Saskatchewan there will once again be an NDP Government.
The Hon. Member mentioned changes to the unemployment insurance. I am thankful he did that because it gives me the opportunity to speak about a change I would like to see to the unemployment insurance, a change which I am trying to promote through the introduction of a Private Member's Motion, which was not drawn unfortunately. I wonder what the Hon. Member's opinion would be of the change I would like to see happen, in addition to some of the positive changes that were made. We in this House think the changes the Government have proposed are on balance a disaster but
The Address-Mr. Schneider
there nevertheless has been some changes that we approve of which the Member mentioned. I wonder why there was not any action with respect to the concern that a great many people have concerning the UI regulations and parents who have children who are terminally ill, children who are in hospital and who have to be visited. Their parents have to be with them day in and day out in this very difficult time in the lives of these families. These are people who often have to leave their jobs. They are not entitled to unemployment insurance.
I have been lobbied in Winnipeg by groups of social workers and other people who work in hospitals in this situation to have a change made to the unemployment insurance scheme which would make allowance for parents who find themselves in this very painful and tragic situation. I was very disappointed that when the Minister had an opportunity to reform the UI system, and if she wanted to appeal to those who want to make the UI system more humane, this was not one of the other things that she undertook.
I wonder whether the Hon. Member would be prepared to get up to support that particular reform at this time.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was heartened somewhat to notice that the Hon. Member way down at the other end of this side of the House made some reference to my ranting and raving. Obviously my statements excited him. I am extremely pleased to know that I could excite anyone down at that end of the room.
He is right. I was a mayor of Regina. He made reference to old, but only in terms of the fact that nine years of service was given by myself to my birthplace. He also made mention of the fact that I am familiar with partisan politics.
I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there seems to be a fair amount of criticism in Regina these days about the unfair comparison between taxes in Regina and Saskatoon. I would say that, yes, I did witness partisan politics for the greater period of the nine years I served there. The majority of my council, while ashamedly admitting they were all members of the New Democratic Party and had philosophies that way, did not admit it during election time. After the election it came out and was truly born. Yes, I am familiar with partisan politics. I watched them for several years.

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Blaikie
I am somewhat disturbed that he counters my claims of distortion with claims of distortion and hence the public is left to sit back in judgment and wonder who to believe.
He mentioned the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act to which I made reference and how glad he was that I had raised it because it gave him an opportunity. I consider that to be somewhat of a weak attempt to talk about anything that any Member wishes to talk about at any time, given the fact that the Throne Speech kept itself open to everything. I am glad he is glad about something.
With respect to his specific point, however, I think that it would be pure folly for any intelligent being to give a yes or no answer to effecting any change of government policy, proposed or otherwise, without having the full opportunity to have an open and intelligent debate leading thereto.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to contribute to the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I see that the Right Hon. the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) is in the House. I am glad about that because most of what I will have to say will pertain to the Government's foreign policy. Perhaps we can have an exchange or two after I am finished.
I would like to begin, though, as is the tradition, with saying how grateful I am to the constituents of the new riding of Winnipeg Transcona for having been reelected. I will just say only this because we have so little time, and I want to give all my time to the Minister.
We know the origin of the name Winnipeg. But the name Transcona is the name of a railway town that was created in 1911 beside the new shops built for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railroad. Transcona literally derives itself from the notion of transconti- nental. Members will not be surprised, therefore, and have not been over the years, at the vehemence with which I defend transcontinental rail passenger service. It literally goes to the veiy heart and history of the community that I grew up in.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: So your continental.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The problem with this Government is that it no longer wants to be transcontinental; it wants to be continental in the north-south sense. However, I will not be distracted.
I would like to address myself to the foreign policy record of the Government. I begin by saying that the Minister knows that on a number of occasions we have had opportunity to co-operate on various issues, but I am going to be critical today because I think the Government deserves a great deal of criticism in a variety of ways.
We know that Canada was just elected to the Security Council of the United Nations. This makes Canada a very important country in the international community. We always have been an important country in the international community, but this gives concrete expression to that importance. It gives Canada a true opportunity to be a leader in the international community, particularly, of course, at the United Nations. It gives Canada the opportunity to be a strong voice for a great many things that need to happen in the world. So my intention here today is to reflect upon just what kind of voice Canada is in the world with respect to international affairs.
As I look over the range of issues which one could talk about I see that the Canadian voice ranges from being in some cases no voice at all to being a hypocritical voice, to being a timid voice, to being a cold war voice, to being a fading voice. I would like to go through all these if I have the time.
What is at stake here is the cumulative erosion of Canada's reputation in the world as a country that shows leadership, as a country that is able to help in many ways to bring about the kind of peace and development that so many Canadians desire for the planet that they live on.
Perhaps I will begin with what I am sure must be a sore spot, even though he cannot admit it, for the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that is, where Canada's voice has turned out to be a hypocritical voice. That of course has to do with South Africa and the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in 1985 stood up before the United Nations and in one of those rhetorical moments that the Prime Minister is so famous for said that if there was no progress toward the ending of apartheid in South Africa Canada would move toward comprehensive mandatory economic sanctions.
April 13, 1989

The world cheered, as did many Canadians. The Prime Minister basked in the glory of that statement for some time. He enjoyed a certain amount of political gain as a result of that statement. However, what has happened is that whatever gain accrued to the Prime Minister was achieved at the expense of Canada's international reputation. Now that the end of apartheid is no closer, that events in South Africa have arguably deteriorated in many respects since the Prime Minister made his statement, particularly with respect to the treatment of anti-apartheid activists in South Africa by the South African Government, and that the Canadian Government has not acted, Canada has been made to look a fool, literally, on the international stage.
I am sure that privately it must really irritate the Secretary of State for External Affairs to have to go around from conference to conference defending the hypocricy of one of his former arch-rivals in the political realm. I do not expect him to comment on that, but this is what I mean when I talk about a hypocritical voice.
When I say a timid voice I am referring to two areas, one in which I think the record of the Government is better than the other. I will start with the better one. It has to do with the Government's approach to Central America. I think the Minister has shown an openness to learning about Central America, appreciating what is going on there and appreciating the deficiencies of American policy in that area that is admirable. However, it has been a timid voice in this respect. The Minister, in the language of the Government, has not been willing to be as explicitly critical of American policy in that area as many people would want him to have been, particularly with respect to the funding of the Contras. Nevertheless, we are now moving to a point where it is conventional wisdom that the United States should no longer fund the invasion of Nicaragua by the Contras.
This is something that Canada could have said a long time ago if it were not so timid a country and if the Government had not been so timid. Could we not have helped that process along much earlier if we had been willing to say that? Having said that, I hope that the Government will try to continue to play the constructive role that it has in the peace process which has been encouraged by the Special Committee on the peace process. I know for instance that the Nicaraguan Gov-
The Address-Mr. Blaikie
ernment is interested in having Canada play a role in the months leading up to and including the election set for February, 1990.1 hope that the Minister will be open to any way in which Canada can be part of the international presence at the Nicaraguan elections, so those elections can be beyond reproach and can be seen to be a legitimate part of the peace process.
I would encourage the Minister at the same time to consider enhancing development assistance to Nicaragua in order to alleviate the severe economic problems that are a result of the war, the embargo and various other things.
I spoke of a timid voice. I am thinking also of the Middle East, Mr. Speaker. Here was a case where the Government was more cautious than the cautious. It was a case of waiting until everyone else had faced up to the changes that had been wrought in the Middle East by the changes in PLO policies. We certainly encouraged the Government, before it did so, to take the steps that it did.
We often criticize the Government for wanting to be in lock-step with the United States on many issues, but here was a case where not only the U.S., but almost everyone else on the block had faced up to this reality, and yet Canada was the last to do so. This again made Canada look far too timid in its way of dealing with these serious regional conflicts.
I have talked about a hypocritical voice and a timid voice. Where there is no voice at all seems to be in NATO one of the various institutions that the Minister and his colleagues like to defend, particularly if they think it is advantageous to them to compare their position to the NDP.
What is the role of Canada within NATO, and when is the Minister going to give us some kind of a comprehensive explanation of what the Government's policy is with respect to the debates that are going on within NATO as to the modernization of nuclear weapons?
I read that the government is in favour of modernization of nuclear weapons. If that is true, I would like to hear what the explanation is and so would the Canadian people. So much is at stake in that debate as to whether or not the Lance missiles are going to be replaced, whether the progress made in the INF treaty is going to be endangered by that kind of modernization.

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Blaikie
There are debates going on in NATO about the adoption of non-provocative defence or non-offensive defence. Where is Canada on this? Are we not part of the debate that is going on about how changes in Europe and east-west relations will be dealt with? Why do we have to be reduced to being a spectator? That is what I mean when I say that in this sense Canada has no voice.
Where we do have a voice it sounds like a cold war voice. There has been no repudiation of what was antiquated then, but what is even more antiquated now i.e. the rhetoric of the foreign policy paper of the Government. I believe it was called challenge and commitment or something like that. This was a document which was widely condemned at the time for being anachronistic, for belonging more to the 1950s than to the 1980s. As a result of events that have happened since then, both in the Soviet Union and in the west, the Government's cold war voice has become even less concerned with reality. Again we hear no updating of that.
I read the speeches that Mrs. Thatcher gave when Chairman Gorbachev came to London. The Government is in danger, in fact has been for some time of being to the right of Thatcher and to the right of Reagan in the last few months of his presidency. One wonders, are we simply waiting for Bush to make up his mind so that Canadians will know where they stand in respect of east-west relations. Or is this an opportunity for us to show some leadership in relationship with our allies instead of meekly assenting to whatever way the United States and NATO wants to use us, whether in the follow on Forces attack strategy which compels us to destroy the livelihood of the land of our Inuit people in Labrador through low-level flight testing or in testing the advance or Stealth Cruise missiles which many people contend could be used as a form of a first strike weapon and therefore is destabilizing? Why do we have to be such uncritical participants in all of this?
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I mention a fading voice. By a fading voice, I am talking about when the Budget comes down on April 27 and whether we will see a significant slashing of Canadian support for overseas development and assistance. This has been the jewel of Canadian foreign policy. It has not been as good as we would like to have seen it. There has never been the percentage of GNP in terms of spending that we would want, but certainly Canada has a reputation abroad of being a country committed to overseas development assistance. I can tell you that many people are very worried. We had the North-South Institute and the Canadian Council on
International Co-operation expressing their concern yesterday. This really could be the straw that breaks the camel's back, Mr. Speaker.
In addition to all the things that I have talked about already where we choose to have no voice, choose to maintain the cold war voice and where we seem to have a hypocritical or timid voice, if our commitment to overseas development assistance is seen to be a fading voice, then the worries that many people have about the way Canada's international reputation is under attack, both because of sins of omission and commission on the part of this Government, will turn out to be true. I think it is a tragedy. In four years you can do some damage, but this Government has got another four years. Unless they change their ways, we will have had eight years of this kind of approach. By that time we will have gone a long way to changing the role of Canada in the world for the worse.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I am tempted to seek unanimous consent to go on and on, but I have a hunch I would not get it. The Member from Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) might give it to me because we gave it to him not long ago, but I cannot be sure of everyone else.
So I look forward to whatever the Minister might have to say. Perhaps we can carry on the debate.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Calgary Northeast (Mr. Kindy) on a question or comment.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comment on the Government's Throne Speech and the Member's speech itself. In the Speech from the Throne, the Government mentions its commitment to NATO and mentions disarmament. I hope for world peace, the initial statement by the two superpowers to reduce nuclear armaments will continue, but we should always keep in mind that nuclear arms have acted as a deterrent for a third world war.
We should encourage President Gorbachev in his efforts to liberalize the Soviet system with perestroika and glasnost and expand our trade relations with countries as long as they respect human rights. Therefore we should reconfirm our commitment to the Helsinki Agreement on human rights and monitor those countries that don't adhere to it. We should applaud the fact that the Soviet Union removed itself from Afganistan. I hope that this soon will happen in Lebanon where we have foreign troops, Israeli and others occupying that country. On the Palestinian question, our Government makes no mention of the fact that Israel has occupied that part of the world for many years and there is a constant human rights violation there. We should con-
April 13, 1989

demn such action and be part of the world community that expresses its condemnation at the United Nations.
We should also press for an international peace conference on the Middle East issue so as to bring justice to the oppressed people of Palestine. I hope the Hon. Member who just spoke would comment on the Palestinian issue.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did comment on the Palestinian issue in the early part of my speech. We have supported the call for an international conference.
The Hon. Member quoted sentences from the Throne Speech in which the Government welcomed the progress between the superpowers. On the other hand he talked about the need to maintain a strong nuclear deterrent and so on. That is part of the problem. I believe we will not be able to respond adequately to the diplomatic initiatives, as well as others taken by the Soviet Union, if we do not show that we too are willing to change our way of thinking.
I agree that it is a difficult process to decide what action one should take and when, but I am very concerned that the West might be sending the wrong signal, that is, that it is not prepared to move and that it will be all give and no take. That is a concern.
The Hon. Member talked about the Soviet Union. I had an opportunity recently to be in Moscow with other parliamentarians for a Conference on Ecological Problems in the North. This is another area I would have dealt with had I the time. Environmental co-operation between Canada and the Soviet Union is another way in which we can begin to co-operate in the North and in other ways.
The whole question of the global environment is something that must be taken seriously. I got the impression that the Soviet Union is taking the problem seriously, possibly because serious environmental problems are coming home to roost there. I almost detected a sense of panic in their voice about the environment. Whatever sins we may have committed here, I have the feeling they have done some things I would rather not know about.
The Address-Mr. Blaikie
There is an opportunity for co-operation in the North and elsewhere that I hope will some day trivialize the differences we have had over the years. There is a need for planetary solidarity, a global human solidarity for the survival of us all. I suggest that that struggle for survival will make some of the divisions that we have experienced over the last 40 years seem quite trivial. I hope they will become trivial as changes take place in the Soviet Union and we respond intelligently to them, moving toward a world which is no longer divided between these two armed camps contemplating its destruction.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was tempted to miss the opportunity for debate but I do not want to do that. I was interested by the one word to which the Hon. Member consistently referred. That was the word "voice". He characterized the role of Canada in the world as being related to our voice and how we express our voice.
Certainly I remember countless occasions on which he has urged me to use Canada's voice to condemn some situation or usually some Government, and usually the American Government. It is a challenge that we have to face if we are realistic about how Canada exercises its influence in the world.
Let us take Central America. It is my view that had I accepted his voice and the voice of his Party over the last couple of years, and had we used our influence to condemn the United States in Central America, that probably would have cost us the capacity to play the very constructive, albeit quite limited and specific role that Canada is able to play in moving that region toward a peace process.
We are there because we have some credentials. In order to maintain those credentials, very often one has to restrain one's voice. One cannot always raise it.
Canada has more to offer the world than advice. We have some very substantial capacities as a nation. We have demonstrated them over time. We have honed them. They are respected very generally, but we can waste them. We can waste them often if we prefer the luxury of expressing an opinion to the harder work of having an effect on actual events.

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Blaikie
I have spoken of Central America. The question that is perhaps of the most division between us has to do with the role of Canada to our allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and to the way we should seek to exert our influence on the changing situation in East-West relations. Obviously there are profound and important changes in the Soviet Union. Obviously, as has been demonstrated in Poland and is evident in Hungary and elsewhere, there are important changes in other East Bloc countries.
How do we best encourage those changes while respecting Canadian interests and the values and interests that people have lived and died for in this country and in the Western Alliance for a long time? We certainly cannot assume that perestroika has extended, for example, to the Soviet military. We certainly cannot ignore the continuing build-up in Soviet military preparation in the Kola Peninsula and elsewhere. We cannot be preoccupied with those sorts of things, but neither can we ignore them.
We cannot ignore the reality that the major agreement we have achieved on arms control has been achieved precisely because Canada and other western nations, other NATO nations stayed together to force the Soviet Union to come to negotiation on the INF.
What would have happened had Canada chosen the luxury of expressing a voice rather than being part of the NATO consensus that led to the INF Agreement? Had Canada split from the NATO alliance, would we have had the INF Agreement? I think the likelihood is that we would not.
Those are the kinds of decisions that Canadian policy makers have to confront, precisely because we have more influence in the world than simply a voice. I think the disagreement between the Hon. Member and myself-and I think it is a disagreement reflected in our two Parties-concerns whether we focus on expressing an opinion, which is easy, or whether we attempt the hard work of trying to effect actual changes in difficult complex situations.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Minister chose to comment. I will certainly tiy to reply.
We do have a difference of opinion, a difference of opinion with respect to the historical analysis of some of the issues to which he referred. I will begin with Central America.
I think it is a caricature of the argument to say that it is simply a choice between expressing an opinion which,
according to the Minister is easy, and doing the quiet constructive work that the Minister always talks about. Sometimes expressing an opinion is a very difficult thing if the person or country one is expressing an opinion about will be unhappy with that opinion, as the Americans would have been if the Minister had chosen to express an opinion about the U.S. funding of Contras when we asked him to do so. If the Minister believes that would have been easy, I think he would have to reconsider his argument.
I suggest the reason he did not express an opinion at that time is that it would have been very difficult, not easy, but had we expressed that opinion earlier we may have been part of that group of countries which eventually caused the United States to rethink its position.
It was ultimately Oscar Arias of Costa Rica, which is much more dependent on U.S. aid than Canada, who was willing to say that the Contras should not be funded by the United States. Surely if Costa Rica could take such a step, dependent as it is on the United States, we could have done so. We are not that dependent on the United States yet, although we may be after the Free Trade Agreement has been in place for some time. However, we have that independence now and have not used it.
The Minister talks about East-West relations and says that we cannot ignore the reality of the build-up in the Kola Peninsula and so on. I am not asking him to do that. I am not asking him to ignore any reality but to be part of the new reality. We should take an active, conscious, intelligent debating role in that new reality. Instead the Minister is perceived to be simply a spectator to that debate. If that is a wrong perception, I hope he will show me how. Every time someone tries to engage in the debate, the Minister pours cold water on the debate by caricaturing the debate instead of entering into the very difficult arguments involved.
I am glad to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is here, a very unusual event, Mr. Speaker. I hope it was foreign policy that brought him into the House of Commons and some of my remarks about his hypocritical stance with respect to South Africa and the fact that he has made a fool of Canada on the world stage by saying one thing about South Africa and doing another or not doing what he said he would do if apartheid did not come to an end.
April 13, 1989

I welcome the Prime Minister's intervention in this debate. We could really have some fun if he would get to his feet.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. friend for his kind reference to me. I am here because when I heard that he was speaking, I rushed down from my office.
I want to tell the Hon. Member to check Hansard. He will see that our good friend and his colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin), pointed out in Hansard some years ago, watching me come to the House of Commons, that he had been in the House since 1968 and that I was the first Prime Minister who came regularly to listen to him as I wanted to listen to my hon. friend. I just wanted to put that on the record in case my hon. friend wants to become less bellicose and more peaceful as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and I are on these matters.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, do I get a chance to respond? You keep turning on the mike behind me. I do not want to turn my back on the House of Commons in order to speak.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) referred to a remark made by the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin), a remark he probably made when he was still the Hon. Member for Regina West. Being in the House is something that the Prime Minister should do more often. It is a habit that I thought he was falling away from.
If this is the beginning of re-engaging the House of Commons and being present for debates, I would submit that that is a welcome trend. It is about time that more Members were present in the House of Commons and that we did have real debates between each other and not proxy debates through Hansard. If the Prime Minister's presence here is an attempt to encourage that, then all the better, as far as I am concerned.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to to have this honour and opportunity to respond to the Speech from the Throne and to take part in the debate that has been going on this past number of days. I would also like at this time to thank those constituents I have represented for the past four years for the confidence they have placed in me again, as we look forward to another term of office, to represent the views and concerns of Canadians from western Canada.
The Address-Mr. Porter
The foundations of some of the initiatives outlined in the Throne Speech were established during the Thirty-third Parliament. One of those was building a stronger economy. Canada has seen the creation of 1.4 million jobs since 1984. This country's economic indicators have led the way among western industrialized nations. Maintaining that economic performance is essential and it will not be easy in a competitive world with inflation and interest rates under pressure.
We are closely tied economically through liberalized trade and commerce between nations. That is a fact of life in today's world. There is no doubt that events taking place in our global economy have an immediate effect on Canada. An example of that effect, which affects us all and certainly those in my constituency of Medicine Hat, is world energy prices. A movement of one dollar up or down results in a change of $150 million in income in the Province of Alberta and that has a ripple effect throughout that economy and that of all Canada.
As a result of the agricultural trade war, primarily between the United States and the EEC, we have seen grain prices halved in some cases. Several years of drought have exacerbated the situation in western Canada. No Government can offset the damage caused by droughts and by volatile world oil prices, but in the past four years this Government has implemented programs that have certainly helped, and they have helped a lot. There has been over $10 billion in assistance to agriculture in the last four years.
I have been involved in agriculture all of my life and I have seen droughts before. I do not recall a special grain program in the past. I do not remember a $1 billion drought package. The outlook is a little better this spring. Conditions relating to that drought still linger on. I hope it does start to rain, not so much for me but for my little grandson who will be four this fall. He has never seen rain out there before.
I would be the first to acknowledge that we have to continue to work toward some long-term agricultural policies. We have done a number of things, including tripartite stabilization programs and improvements to grain stabilization where modifications have been made. New programs and initiatives have to be carried out, they have to be voluntary and they have to be actuarially sound. I think the Grains 2000 option is something that is well worth consideration.

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Porter
What concerns me, and I am sure most Canadians, is how we maintain let alone improve existing programs and social policies if we do not address the greatest impediment to our future, Canada's national debt. Like many of us sitting here, I have heard all the statistics, I have listened to the debate about our national debt, about when it got started, about how it grew, about whose fault it was. There has even been some pointed remarks about who fathered it. I do not think it matters at this point who fathered the debt, but somebody has to look after the baby.
A lot of things could have been done and should have been done. In 1978, the national debt was around $60 billion. It may be just a coincidence, but that is roughly the amount of funding that came out of western Canada as a result of the National Energy Program. I think many things could have been done with the debt at that time. Unfortunately, we cannot make hindsight retroactive.
As we discuss who is to blame, the debt continues to grow and we all have a share in it. That includes everyone in this House and each Canadian every one of us represents. We constantly hear complaints about someone not getting their fair share. Provinces do not get their fair share, special interest groups are not looked after, your constituency gets more than mine. Believe me, we all have a piece of the action when it comes to sharing the national debt. Anyone who has given any serious thought to where this country is headed has to be concerned. My constituents of Medicine Hat are concerned and I am sure Members on both sides of the House are hearing the same concerns.
Since 5.40 yesterday afternoon, this Government will have had to raise $88 million to pay for the interest on that debt. Since 4.40 today, the Government will have had to come up with $3.6 million. If you give me my allocation of time, Mr. Speaker, it will show that talk is not cheap. It will have cost all of us $1.2 million to service that debt.
Where does the money come from? I guess most of it comes from that 31 cents out of eveiy tax dollar that each of us sends in to Revenue Canada. There are no simple or easy answers. We could get rid of the debt next week if every Canadian man, woman and child sent Revenue Canada a cheque for $12,300. If they sent $100 a month, it would pay the interest. I think there are two chances of that happening, one slim and one fat.
If, through some quirk of circumstance, Members on both sides of the House agree to freeze all spending at today's level, the interest payments alone would double the national debt by 1995. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that the Members who will occupy this Chamber in 1995 will find the situation any easier to deal with than those of us who are here today? Eight years from now, unless the debt is reduced, the Government will be paying more interest than it currently collects from total personal income taxes from all Canadians.
Rising interest rates are one of the major concerns in my constituency. They add to the price of consumer goods, they cripple small business, they hurt agriculture, they make owning a home or maintaining a mortgage in many cases impossible. Many people remember and are still paying the bills for interest charges of the late 1970s when no effort was made to address the problem. The strength or weakness of our overall economy has an influence on interest rates. Inflation plays a major role. Monetary and economic policies beyond our borders are a factor.
The greatest stimulus to rising interest is our reluctance to come to grips with our national debt. We all know the best place to cut is some expensive federal program, Crown corporation or tax incentive, but let us make the cut where it does not affect me, my family, business, profession, or even my province. Let us have it anywhere else, but let us go for it. The present economic performance and the future economic potential of Canada cannot be sustained if this fiscal indulgence continues to grow.
One area I want to touch on from the Throne Speech is that of the environment. I have raised cattle most of my life. Like most people in that industry, I have developed a close appreciation and respect for environmental issues. You learn to survive and treat the short-grass area of western Canada's Palliser triangle with utmost respect. It is a harsh, unforgiving region for those who abuse it. This land is so fragile that the tracks left by the wagons of earlier settlers can still be seen today. The trails left by thousands of buffalo on their way to water holes still remain. The last signs of a people who took no more from the land than they needed and left it as they found it are still out there on those broad prairies in the form of circles of stone known as tepee rings.
April 13, 1989

Mother Nature and Father Time can be a fickle pair. They have their own laws; they make their own rules. They are not enforced by legislation nor are they enshrined in any constitution; but we break them at our peril, and the penalties are swift and harsh.
In a time of high technology, fax machines in our offices, mobile phones in our cars, satellites in space, perhaps we should remind ourselves that our very existence on this planet depends on a six-inch layer of topsoil, a little rain, the good Lord and the people who husband this fragile, productive and renewable natural resource. We cannot continue to treat it as we have been. To quote from the Speech from the Throne: "Canadians possess a unique sense of their relationship to the land, whose rich, vast diversity has shaped their values and experiences".
This Government can continue to produce the economic, cultural values that this country of ours has become renowned for. We must work together to make this happen. We are in a very difficult time.
I touched on two issues that are of concern. There are no doubt many more. Every Hon. Member in this House has a concern that affects those you represent. On a global scale, we have concerns with the Uruguay Round of GATT and the effects it will have. In the industry I represent, we need changes to the Meat Import Act so producers trading in the North American market are dealing with the same rules. We are not asking for favours. Canadians can be competitive with any producer or manufacturer in the world, provided they have the opportunity. Those of us in government must ensure that Canadians have the opportunity to bring out the best in themselves and their country.
I want to thank the House for its indulgence. I am confident the Throne Speech tabled the other day will lead the way for this Government to bring about the important changes needed in Canada for all of us and those we represent.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I heard the Hon. Member mention the punitive link between the large federal debt and high interest rates. I do not have an economics degree, but I do have a memory. I remember the last time we had tremendously high interest rates was in the early 1980s. Those interest rates fell, right through to 1986 and 1987. This was a time when the federal debt was increasing. While interest rates were going one way, the
The Address-Mr. Gauthier
deficit was going the other. Yet I am told that high debt means higher interest rates. Our experience in this country does not support that contention. On what basis does the Hon. Member attempt to draw that relationship?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not have a degree in economics either, but I have been in business all my life. I have attempted to make things work in the real world. I had to go to banks to borrow money. Do you know today that to put a pound of beef on an animal in a feedlot requires $35 in interest costs alone? Those costs are reflected right through the system. They are passed on to the buying public.
When a government pays the amount of interest we are experiencing today, it has a bearing on the overall picture. Other factors come into play, such as global economies and inflationary pressures. Canadians will have to pay for the large debt in increased taxes and cuts in services that Members opposite do not want to see. The more we pay, the less we spend in other areas. This puts pressure on monetary policy. If I have less to operate my business, the banker is more reluctant to lend money. Pressure on interest rates tends to rise because the banks know there is more risk out there. In time, this will put pressures on us.
I do not understand socialist monetary policies. I hope I never have to. I live about nine miles from the Saskatchewan border. I know what a socialist government has done there. I have noticed what it has done in British Columbia. I do not want my family living under those conditions.
I do appreciate your question. I believe the federal debt and the interest charges it incurs have put pressure on our monetary system.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the Throne Speech pronounced by the Governor General on April 3 when she opened the second session of the thirty-fourth Parliament of Canada. The Government, which of course prepared the speech, seems to have asked some unknown up in the attic of the Langevin Building, on the other side of Wellington, to write something which, as far we can see, is completely detached from the realities of this world and bears no relation to the needs of Canadians.

April 13, 1989
The Address-Mr. Gauthier
If the Prime Minister had just looked out the window on the other side, he would have been very much inspired by the people I have the honour to represent, the people of (Ottawa-Vanier.
There is not a single Member in this House who has not visited my riding. They all know my riding. It is rather special. It is probably the only riding you can reach on foot in a few minutes and which offers good hotels, a convention centre, wonderful museums, an interesting market, courteous and smiling people, and, as in many other ridings, problems that are difficult to solve, because we also have our poor, our needy, our drug addicts, all those people who depend on us for their survival. I have two soup kitchens, Meals on wheels, I have two places where people can get some food, so-called food banks. It isn't easy for a society to admit that it has to dispense food in a country as rich, as full of resources, and as envied as ours.
Mr. Speaker, at the foot of Parliament Hill, just a five-minute walk away, mothers are looking for decent shelter for their children. There are the unemployed and senior citizens-there are 7,500 in my riding-senior citizens who had a difficult time, having experienced the Depression and two World Wars, and now, in many cases, depend on us today for their food and board. There are young people who have lost hope and are involved in drugs and prostitution. They are among the most disadvantaged in our society. They are the forgotten, the neglected Canadians.
Today, our social safety net, and more specifically, our unemployment insurance system, is increasingly at risk because it is in the hands of a Government that does not understand. In my riding they would say this is a Government without a heart.
In the Throne Speech, the Government claimed it wanted to improve the unemployment insurance program's, and I quote:
. . .effectiveness and its fairness.
Now that they have shown their true colours and have proposed their amendments, I cannot help wondering, quite sincerely: Who and what do they have in mind?
I know the number of jobless will increase, as the number of welfare recipients, which will in fact go up dramatically in the next few months. I also know that people will have to wait in line in front of the Sainte-Bri-gitte Center, in my riding, or in front of the soup kitchen
and the Salvation Army where the poor seek haven, people who have no shelter, no place to sleep.
The government has not clearly defined its goals. They want, on the one hand, to tighten the rules in order to limit the number of workers eligible to UI benefits. Workers will have to work longer before becoming eligible and then they will receive fewer benefits. Unable to get unemployment insurance benefits, the jobless through no fault of theirs will wind up on welfare. As we know, Mr. Speaker, welfare services are a provincial responsibility. So, the government is in fact transfering to the provinces a difficult human problem instead of closely exmining it.
Moreover, the expenses incurred by the provinces for welfare will not appear on the balance-sheet of the federal government. Instead, its financial statements may show that they were successful in reducing the deficit. But in fact the public will be misguided because of a little game of hide and seek. The government is passing a problem on to the provinces when in fact they should have solved it since they have the means to do so, Mr. Speaker.
All in all, the taxpayers will not save a penny. Quite the opposite, since they will probably pay more with the federal tax the government has been promising. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is travelling across the country, saying: 'You can expect a tax hike!" I even remember, Mr. Speaker, the fiscal reform he proposed, and the sales tax which will apply to almost all services.
In my riding, people are concerned because during the election we discussed those problems, they came up during door calls. Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that the proposed sales tax is a problem to them, because it is regressive. It applies to everyone regardless of income level. The poor will pay a sales tax just as the rich. Oh, there is to be income tax credits and sales tax credits, of course there will be a system in place! At home in Ottawa-Vanier, Mr. Speaker, I have people who are honest but do not always understand those forms sent by the Governement that must be filled to quality for all sorts of credits, all sorts of rebates. And often the poor are the losers, because the rich, bankers, businessmen will not hurt-they have accountants who prepare their tax returns. The poor will be the losers, Mr. Speaker, they will be penalized. Unfortunately, we have not yet the resources in place to help those people.
April 13, 1989

In my riding right now, that income tax return is so complex accountants who used to volunteer their services to help senior citizens prepare their returns are telling me this year: "We have no time." It is too complicated! Although they told us they were going to make it simpler for Canadians it is the opposite. They made things more complicated, Mr. Speaker. They finally discouraged those in my riding who used to help people who needed help, seniors who are entitled to income tax credits, the poor who are entitled to income tax credits, and many have-nots who, because they do not understand the documents and forms, do not fill them out and do not apply for credits.
Let me repeat that this Government is hardnosed, Mr. Speaker.
I think we are all aware of the problems, Mr. Speaker.
I see you are preparing to interrupt me. Mr. Speaker, if it were possible, I would like to resume tomorrow morning, as it is 6 p.m.

subtopic: CHILD CARE-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION-REQUEST FOR ACTION
CHILD CARE-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION-REQUEST FOR ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise pursuant to Standing Order 38 to revisit an issue which I raised in this place on April 4 last. I am talking, of course, about the issue of child care.
On that day I called upon the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty) to introduce comprehensive child care legislation in order to address the critical situation that has arisen. It is a situation critical not just for families right across this country, but also
Adjournment Debate
critical for the child care profession in general. My concern stems from a reference that was made in the Speech from the Throne delivered by the Governor General in the other place, and its scant mention of the Government's commitment to child care.
The relevant passage reads as follows: "The Government remains committed to a national child care program". What is of great concern to all Canadians is what the Government truly means by a national child care program. Does this refer to Bill C-144 as it was tabled in the last Parliament? I devoutly hope not. The vast majority of Canadian child care workers and parent groups alike rejected most of the Government's proposals as laid out in that Bill.
I am particularly concerned that the views that were expressed by these groups, from Vancouver to my own riding of Halifax, will continue to go unnoticed and ignored. Even a cursory glance at some of this testimony will underline deeply the rationale behind the recommendations and proposals that all these groups put forward. I will deal with some of these proposals later.
First, I would like to paint a clearer picture of the current status of child care in Canada. Almost two million Canadian children need child care outside the home, some part time, some full time. Under the present system only 10 per cent of those two million children can be accommodated. A staggering number of parents look for such care in vain. The remaining 90 per cent of children who are in need of child care are either looked after by relatives, friends, or babysitters, or unlicensed caregivers, or they are simply left alone, the latch-key children that we hear so much about. These statistics are profoundly disturbing. In 1987 the percentage of children under the age of 13 in licensed child care in Canada was remarkably low.
Let me give a few examples based on 1987 figures provided by the National Council of Welfare. In Newfoundland, where there are currently 30,998 children under the age of 13, only 1,318 of these children are being cared for by licensed child care services. In other words, 96 per cent of Newfoundland children under the age of 13 cannot be accommodated, should the need arise. Similar figures are equally disturbing in my home Province of Nova Scotia, where there are 48,298 children under the age of 13, some 42,901 of whom do not enjoy the possibility of a licensed quality child care space.

April 13, 1989
Adjournment Debate
In other words, 89 per cent of Nova Scotia's children under the age of 13 cannot expect the benefit of quality care if and when their primary caregiver must work outside the home. What this points to is a gaping child care crisis which will not be cured by vague promises and half-hearted commitments.

Our day-care centers are in a state of crisis. Last Friday, in Montreal, a great many of the 2 000 CNTU-af-filiated workers of various day-care centers went on strike for a day to show how impatient and concerned they were about the present situation Mr. Speaker, an action plan or a bill is needed to meet the needs of day-care center operators and those of all Canadian families.

It is clear that we have a crisis on our hands and that we need immediate action to deal with it. In the few minutes that remain I would like to briefly describe how we find ourselves in this situation and, second, to offer some remedies and suggestions about how we might end the crisis if the political will exists. Sadly the Government's commitment to child care has been, to say the least, intermittent.
In March 1987, the Special Committee on Child Care tabled its final report. The Conservative majority within that committee called for more grants to parents through the tax system in what they called giving parents a greater choice. They simply did not realize, nor does it appear as if they realize now, that this was an inadequate and meaningless solution.
What is needed is more child care spaces. Nine months after the special parliamentary committee tabled its final report, the Government responded by announcing its national child care strategy, three components of which were the following: a $100 million child care special initiatives fund to promote research and development activities in child care, federal-provincial cost sharing arrangements which would increase the number of child care spaces over seven year, and a set of tax measures to increase the annual child care deduction from $2,000 to $4,000 annually.
Since the election the Government has had nearly five months to develop a national child care plan that would incorporate the suggestions and proposals put forward by
many interest groups across Canada. After the Throne Speech the Minister of National Health and Welfare, when pressured to state his Government's commitment to a national child care program, responded by saying: "We are continuing to study the issue, but we have nothing to announce at the present time".
I know there are tens of thousands of families out there today who are wondering how long the Minister has to continue studying this matter which has been studied and analysed for years. When is the Government going to commit itself through legislation to a real national child care program that responds to the real needs of all Canadians. The solutions are there. What is left is for the decisions-
