subtopic: CHILD CARE-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION-REQUEST FOR ACTION
speechtext:
Today, Mr. Speaker, the first time I am called upon to reply as Parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I want first of all to congragulate the Hon. Member for Halifax (Mrs. Clancy) on her being elected to this House on November 21, as well as her appointment as a Party critic on women issues. I am sure she must have been flabbergasted by the approach Liberal had taken to the day-care bill before the House adjourned.
I am sure that in her own riding, before the election, she must have found it absolutely horrible, because she is referring now to a crisis situation, and she might be right to do so; however, I should like to remind our audience that this crisis has been brought to a head by the attitude of a Liberal non-elected Senate who deliberately stopped this Bill before the election. She may say "Ah!" but that is the sad truth, Mr. Speaker.
Also, I urge the Hon. Member to be twice as vigilant, because the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) has just announced a reform of the Unemployment Insurance scheme which will greatly help women, especially in the areas of maternity leave and training programs; and she knows as well as I do that Canadian women, those in my riding, in the province of Quebec and the city of Halifax, need training and re-training. If there are people in our society who need that, women do.



April 13, 1989

Since she is the critic on women's issues, I would also strongly urge her to contact the school board in her riding or in her province at Halifax. She might suggest that these school boards apply for funds, because money is available from the special project assistance fund for, among other things, helping schools set up day care facilities, as she said in her remarks.
For example, Mr. Speaker, I might mention that the Minister has just announced a grant of $80,391 to the Leeds-Grenville riding school boards to set up the kind of child care services which meet the needs of families in that area. Mr. Speaker, another grant of $120,645 has been awarded to Quebec's Association des services de garde en milieu scolaire for a study. That is excellent. And then, Mr. Speaker, $422,207 to the Members of the Ottawa region for three assistance fund projects to help organizations find fresh solutions to the child care problem.
Nova Scotia therefore is also entitled to that money, and I would urge the Hon. Member to get in touch with the school boards in her riding and in her province and take full advantage of our Government's generous contribution under the Strategy. Above all, Mr. Speaker, she ought to appeal to the common sense of Senators so they will not unduly delay the legislative measures passed by the House, legitimately elected by Canadians.

subtopic: AIR SAFETY-REVIEW BY DEPARTMENTAL AUDIT BRANCH-MINISTER'S INTENTIONS
AIR SAFETY-REVIEW BY DEPARTMENTAL AUDIT BRANCH-MINISTER'S INTENTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 6, I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) what preparations his Department made in anticipation of the removal of government controls in the airline industry.
The question was not answered by the Minister. I come here before you this evening, Mr. Speaker, in an attempt to receive an answer. I thank you for the opportunity to requestion the Minister on an issue that is vital to the air safety of travellers who use these facilities in Canada.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, the air corridors in our country are congested. The congestion causes safety problems around busy airports, airports where planes are headed especially during peak periods, airports such as Pearson International Airport.
Adjournment Debate
The situation is not improving. It is deteriorating. The Minister refuses in the face of overwhelming evidence to do anything to change these unsafe conditions.
The major airlines of Canada because of deregulation have been able to create what is known as the hub-and-spoke concept, the hub being the major airport and the spokes being those arms that extend to smaller communities. Some of the spoke communities are communities such as Thunder Bay-Nipigon, the region which I represent, Sault Ste. Marie, Winnipeg, Dryden and Windsor, areas such as these that funnel their aircraft into Pearson.
Since Pearson is a major international airport the traffic is further congested because it is a recipient of many international flights, as well as many flights that generate in other areas in Canada. Pearson can be referred to, and often is, as a main hub in all of Canada.
What bothers me, and I know it bothers many other Canadians from smaller communities, is that this hub-and-spoke concept has deteriorated the quality of air travel in the country without the approval of most Canadians. If you book a flight, Mr. Speaker, to one of these centres I have mentioned through one of the two major airlines available to us, you stand a very good chance of ending up on an airline to which you have no contractual relationship. The plane is much smaller than expected. Even in Toronto one has to go outside the airport and across the tarmac in rain or snowy conditions and climb the steps to get on the airplane. This is very unsafe for our aged and handicapped people.
Although these airlines try to offer the services that the larger airlines offer, services such as beverage services, meals and luggage services, it is physically impossible for them to do this. In fact, many of these aircraft do not have any washrooms. If they do, there are not enough to facilitate the number of passengers on the aircraft.
I can go on and on about these deficiencies on these smaller airlines, but the thing that really hurts me and hurts most Canadians from rural Canada and smaller centres is the very fact that when we book on these flights we pay the very same price as we would pay on an airline that offers a more sophisticated service, especially if it is on one of the airlines in Canada or on the international scene that has a competitive route.

April 13, 1989
Adjournment Debate
Airline travel in Canada for rural Canadians and Canadians from smaller centres has gone back at least 20 years. The responsibility for this falls directly on the shoulders of the present Government. Once again another institution of the country is sacrificed at the expense of rural and small town Canada.
What is of greater concern is the fact that most of these smaller airlines expanded operations or began operations as a result of deregulation or the operation of the hub-and-spoke concept. This leads me to the question I asked the Minister which he refused to answer. His own internal documents state that he lacked enough inspectors to protect the very safety of Canadians. The document states that regulatory reform of the domestic airline industry was introduced at a time when the Department possessed neither sufficient trained resources, the required planning and operational processes, nor the necessary enforcement capability required to monitor effectively and foster aviation industry compliance with established safety legislation, safety regulations and safety standards.
The Minister has failed to tell Canadians what he intends to do with respect to the safety of air travel in Canada. The Minister said in this House that decisions will be made without delay on the basis of air traffic safety. The air traffic situation is currently unsafe and getting worse. No measures thus far have improved the safety to the Canadian air traveller.
I ask my question again. When will the Minister address air safety with the urgency Canadians expects?

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AIR SAFETY-REVIEW BY DEPARTMENTAL AUDIT BRANCH-MINISTER'S INTENTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by reiterating something the Minister has repeatedly stated both in this House and outside the House. Canadian skies are safe. To suggest otherwise is both reprehensible and irresponsible, and as such most unworthy of any Member of the House.
I also want to mention that I fly on those small airlines, those commuter feeder lines that serve many parts of the country. I feel very secure and safe because of the care, consideration and individual attention that they give to us as travellers when we are travelling so frequently across the country. I use them every week. I am very pleased that we have the commuter lines because they do provide a necessary service with a very small aircraft which carries often as few as 19 passengers.
On March 29, 1989, the Minister announced the appointment of Justice Estey to review the entire record of the Gander accident investigation with a view to advising the Minister on whether any further investigation or inquiry is warranted. The Minister also announced the appointment of Justice Moshansky to conduct a judicial inquiry into the Dryden accident. These measures were taken in response to the concerns raised about the Canadian Aviation Safety Board which has served to undermine the confidence of Canadians in the board.
In addition, the Minister has reintroduced and referred to the standing committee Bill C-2 an Act to establish the transportation accident investigation board.
Furthermore, while the Minister and his senior officials believe that the inspection resources of the Department of Transport are adequate to the present requirement, nevertheless, the Minister intends to avail himself of the expertise of both industry and government to assist him in ensuring that we have the right resources and that they are used in the right way in order to meet the changing needs of the future.
With specific reference to Lester B. Pearson Airport in Toronto, I would remind Hon. Members that Ministers have just completed two weeks of extensive consultations which will lead to the development of a comprehensive plan for the whole of the southern Ontario airspace. An announcement will be made in due course.
I would like to emphasize that while we do have a shortage of air traffic controllers at Toronto the traffic flow is always matched to the controllers' ability to safely handle the traffic. This means delays, not a decrease in the level of safety.
I would also like to assure Members and the travelling public that every conceivable effort is being made to rectify the shortage situation.

Mr. Speaker, I put a question to the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) on April 5, asking him if the Government was going to pay the amounts which it promised for drought assistance last November 10.
In that press release of last November 10, it said that it would pay $40 to $45 per acre of wheat in western Canada for the maximum drought damage per acre. In eastern Canada it said it would pay from $50 to $57 per acre where the total crop was lost for com and soybeans.
April 13, 1989

The Minister announced some time after that that he was going to pay about 70 per cent in the interim payment.
Since the election is over it has gotten very fuzzy exactly whether it is still $40 or $45. Also, the total amount is fuzzy. I did an open-line show with the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds during the election campaign which was broadcast across Manitoba and Saskatchewan. At that time he said the $850 million was not a cap, that it was just a notional amount of what the Government thought it might be. If it was more than that, based on $40 or $45 per acre, then the Government would pay the extra amount.
More recently it has been very hard to pin the Government down. Is the $850 million a cap? Is it going to pay the full amount?
Thus I put a question to the Minister in this regard and his response was this: "The estimates that we talked about last fall stand exactly the same. Nothing has changed".
He did not say a maximum of $45 per acre in western Canada for wheat loss occurred. He did not say that they were going to pay up to $57 for corn in Ontario, as he said in his press release. It is a great concern that he said last fall that the interim payment was to be at 70 per cent. The interim payment in western Canada was only $12.
Maybe the Government is going to welsh on this deal. Maybe it is only going to pay $20 and say to the provinces, "you pick up half". There was a great kerfuffle. When the Minister announced the program, he said he was going to try to rope in the provinces, but he had not consulted with them. The provinces, even the Tory provinces, said they were not paying any of his campaign promises.
What we would like to get tonight from the Parliamentary Secretary is a clear, unequivocal statement that there is no cap at $850 million. It is going to be based on $40 or $45 maximum in the West and $57 in the East. We want it very clearly spelled out.
This has really been a bollix. They sent out application forms to some people and not to others. Why did they not send out an application to everybody with a Wheat Board quota book and allow individual farmers to make a statutory declaration of what their crop losses were? It could easily be checked against the crop insurance data. Instead they are saying "if you lose more than 15 per cent, then you get a certain percentage based on crop
Adjournment Debate
insurance data". However, they are not saying what that data is.
Is it based on the last five years? Is it based on the last 10 years for each township? That is not clear, so nobody knows really where they are. The whole system has really been bollixed.
The drought was last May, June and July. The loss of crop was last August and September. There is no money. Until now farmers have been getting $12 an acre in the West and $16 for the most severe in the East, and the rest comes in July. We do not know what that other amount is going to be.
The Parliamentary Secretary is one of the most outstanding soybean growers in southwestern Ontario, and he knows what his farmers feel about this. They want to know exactly what the deal is, what the amounts are and when they are going to be paid. I just hope that these matters will be cleared up because many farmers are confused.
I recall that our caucus met with the officials of the Department of Agriculture over a month ago. The Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Vanclief) had a number of farmers, I believe a couple of dozen, who had not received an application form. He sent in their names for application forms, and they just starting to get them now. That is a month ago. According to the data which came out for the program, they had to file their applications by March 15. I think we met with the Department about three or four days before that. Many farmers had not yet received their application forms, and those application forms were to be made and filed with the Department by the fifteenth.
This program has been badly handled. The drought was last year. Cash is coming very late. It should have all been on the table by at least January, February or March when the farmers were putting together the funding for this year's crop. I certainly hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to clarify that the deal is exactly the same, the amounts are the same as they were last fall and not just these estimates that we talked about then. Estimates of what? Farmers want to know where they are, whether they are going to be paid and when they are going to be paid.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased once again to try to provide detail on the effective efforts by this Government to deliver the Drought Assistance Program to Canadian farmers.

April 13, 1989
Adjournment Debate
I would like to say to my hon. friend that it is white beans, not soybeans, but we will let him get away with that.
He is an outstanding grower of white beans.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I would like to say to him also that the deadline for the application has been extended and is flexible for receiving some of those application. The Drought Assistance Program will help producers that were hurt very badly in the 1988 drought. This Government is making every effort to deliver a program that treats producers in many different circumstances fairly, and it is very difficult to find a plan that treats them fairly.
We anticipate that about 120,000 producers may qualify for drought assistance, with over 100 different crops in over 45 different townships. It takes time to develop and deliver a program that deals with so many producers in so many different types of circumstances.
The Canadian Drought Assistance Program administration is working hard to deliver this program to Canadian farmers. More than 145 people are directly involved in its delivery including people on a toll-free line who have been answering up to 4,000 calls a week. Recently in response to the number of phone calls, we doubled the number of operators on the toll-free line to 20 people.
The administration is putting interim payments into the hands of producers as quickly as possible. About 4,500 townships have been designated as drought areas on the basis of preliminary provincial crop insurance data. More drought areas may be designated when final data is available from provincial crop insurance agencies in May.
Personalized applications have been mailed to about 120,000 producers in designated drought areas, and about 100,000 forms have been returned to date.
I am pleased to inform the House, Mr. Speaker, that close to 19,000 interim cheques worth $80 million have been mailed so far to producers. About 65,000 producers will get interim payments. The payments will average $4,300 and will total about $280 million. The timing of these interim payments is similar to the timing of interim payments under last year's Special Canadian Grains Program. Final payments are scheduled to be mailed in July.
We are making progress in other aspects of the program, too. A method for delivering assistance to Ontario horticultural producers has been established. We are working with horticultural groups in other provinces now to establish a method for making payments. Progress is being made with the Province of Quebec on a proposal for program delivery. Discussions are continuing with the provinces on cost sharing.
In addition, I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that producer review committees will be established in each province. This program may be rather complex, but it is resulting in the individual tailoring of payments and an accurate assessment of each producer's needs. The Canada Crop Drought Assistance Program is fair, well targeted and timely. It is being delivered effectively by this Government.
It takes patience, but we have to recognize that many crops in this country are not harvested in June and July of any year. We have many crops that are not harvested until the end of our calendar year which would be the first of December, and very often not delivered. It is very difficult to establish the amount of profit that has been delivered. Those things all take time.
